title: Falcons 53-man roster projection: Can they keep 4 quarterbacks? Who'll make cut at CB? The Falcons must cut their 90-man roster to 53 players by Sunday evening. Here's our final projection for who those 53 will be. Josh Kendall 10
summary:

The Atlanta Falcons wrapped up their preseason at 2-1 with a 17-12 win over the Dolphins in Miami on Friday night. Final rosters must be submitted to the league office by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, so it’ll be a busy flight home for
full_text:
Rookie tight end Jack Velling had four receptions for 30 yards and a touchdown on Friday night but faces an uphill battle to make the team. Carmen Mandato / Getty Images
The Atlanta Falcons wrapped up their preseason at 2-1 with a 17-12 win over the Dolphins in Miami on Friday night. Now, for the hard part — as the Falcons and the rest of the league must cut their 90-man rosters to 53. Final rosters must be submitted to the league office by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday, so it’ll be a busy flight home for coach Kevin Stefanski, general manager Ian Cunningham and president of football Matt Ryan.
“I loved the effort tonight,” Stefanski said afterward. “I was just telling the team how appreciative I am of the effort from April until tonight. I’d love to keep everybody, but Roger Goodell won’t allow it.”
Before we dive into the names on our 53-man roster projection, there are two tricky issues worth noting.
The first is how many quarterbacks the Falcons will keep. I never would have dreamed coming into training camp that the number might be four, but here we are.
Then there’s the injury question. It’s possible that players like defensive lineman Da’Shawn Hand, offensive lineman Kyle Hinton and possibly even cornerback Billy Bowman Jr. will have to start the season on IR or the PUP list, where they don’t count against the 53-man roster. I’ve made my list based on my projections because the Falcons haven’t shared much about injury timelines during training camp. (James Pearce Jr. will go on the reserve/suspended list to begin serving his eight-game suspension and won’t count against the 53 until he returns.)
Projecting the practice-squad players is just a way to open myself up to being wrong — a lot — but I’ve added those, too.
In: Tua Tagovailoa, Michael Penix Jr., Cooper Rush, Jack Strand
Four quarterbacks on a 53-man roster is a lot, but the Falcons are facing a dilemma. Strand, despite being a fantastic story and a very intriguing prospect, is not ready to play in a regular-season game, and the No. 3 QB on this roster has to be ready to play because of the health history of the top two quarterbacks. Atlanta could try to put Strand on the practice squad, but he could then be claimed by another team. The claiming team would have to add him to its 53-man roster, so that might not happen, but the Falcons probably shouldn’t take that risk at a position with so much potential upside.
Tagovailoa started Friday night’s game against the Dolphins and finished 7-for-8 for 95 yards. Penix was cleared for 11-on-11 practice work this week but said he didn’t feel ready for live action. He will be ready in time for the Sept. 13 season opener if he wins the starting job, he said.
In: Bijan Robinson, Brian Robinson, Tyler Goodson
Practice squad: Cash Jones
The biggest question in this room is not whether Goodson has made the team but whether he has done enough to be the No. 2. The fourth-year pro has never had more than 153 rushing yards in a season, but he has been explosive throughout the preseason. In addition to being one of Atlanta’s main kick returners, expect Goodson to get carries this year. He had two catches for 36 yards Friday night. Bijan Robinson dressed but did not play against the Dolphins.
In: Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus, Zachariah Branch, Chris Blair
Practice squad: Dylan Drummond, Beaux Collins
If you think of this wide receiver room like a basketball team, Zaccheaus and Branch are the guards, Dotson is the wing and Blair and London are the post players. The most interesting question about this group is how much London will line up in the slot versus outside. Under Arthur Smith in his first two seasons, London was outside on more than 80 percent of his snaps, according to TruMedia. Under Zac Robinson the last two years, he was in the slot for at least 35 percent of his snaps each season. Moving London around makes it harder for defenses to plan for him, but with Zaccheaus and Branch both best suited for the slot position, London may go back toward his early usage trends. (For the record, he says he doesn’t care where he lines up.)
Blair is entering his fourth NFL season and only has one career catch, but he has shown marked improvement during training camp and should factor into this rotation. Drummond has had a solid camp and would be the sixth man here if the Falcons keep six.
In: Kyle Pitts, Charlie Woerner, Austin Hooper
Practice squad: Joshua Simon, Nick Muse
Atlanta has taken a look at a lot of multiple-tight-end formations throughout the spring and summer. I don’t think that equates to keeping four tight ends, but it is a reason they might keep a couple on the practice squad. Any idea that Hooper’s signing might lead to a lesser role for Woerner appears to be wrong. Woerner is going to be very involved in this offense in the same (mostly blocking) role he’s had in the past. Hooper will be the second pass-catching option behind Pitts.
Pitts will be looking to validate the faith the Falcons showed in him with an offseason extension, and he has had a solid camp. If Tagovailoa starts a lot of games, Pitts could put up big numbers because he has been Tua’s favorite safety valve throughout camp.
In: Ryan Neuzil, Chris Lindstrom, Matthew Bergeron, Jake Matthews, Jawaan Taylor, Corey Levin, Michael Jerrell, Ethan Onianwa, Brandon Walton
Practice squad: Wanya Morris, James Brockermeyer, Andrew Stueber
The most surprising thing here might be that Morris is not on my list. Atlanta got the 25-year-old from Kansas City this offseason in a trade. He has started 16 NFL games, but he just hasn’t been in the rotation much during practices. When Morris has practiced, it has been at left tackle — not his usual spot on the right side — and that versatility plus his athleticism and potential probably keep him around on the practice squad.
Jerrell appears to have earned the swing tackle job as the top backup at both outside positions, and Onianwa and Walton both bring inside-outside versatility that will be valuable on game days. Hinton will be in this group if he doesn’t go on IR.
In: Za’Darius Smith, Samson Ebukam, Cameron Thomas, Azeez Ojulari
Practice squad: Bralen Trice
This group looks a lot different than Atlanta hoped it would, and that could prove a critical factor this season. Jalon Walker was lost for the year with an ACL tear, and Pearce was suspended for the first eight games. The Falcons added Smith as a result, and the 11-year veteran with 70.5 career sacks believes he’s ready to contribute significant sack numbers. It would help a ton if he can.
Ebukam and Thomas appear to have established themselves as starters, and Smith will be a designated pass rusher, at least to start. Ojulari, who joined the Falcons this year in free agency, has 32 NFL starts and 22 sacks but has had a quiet camp and is not a lock.
In: Brandon Dorlus, Maason Smith, Zach Harrison, LaCale London, Chris Williams
Practice squad: Carlos Allen Jr., Devonnsha Maxwell, Eric Johnson II
The loss of Hand has hurt this group. The Falcons added him and Smith in the offseason to solidify their run defense, but Hand has missed the last two weeks with a lower-body injury and may have to start the season on IR or PUP. If he’s going to miss extended time, Atlanta might have to add another big body.
Smith has been disruptive throughout camp, and if he can have a breakout year, it would be a huge boost for the defense. Dorlus already had his breakout year with 8.5 sacks last year. He needs to build on that.
In: Divine Deablo, Christian Harris, Kendal Daniels, Harold Perkins Jr., Josh Woods
Practice squad: JD Bertrand, Daveren Rayner
It looks like we can start thinking of Kendal Daniels as a starter now. The fourth-round rookie initially looked like he would get worked into the rotation slowly behind Harris, but Daniels continues to get practice snaps and praise from his teammates and coaches. By starting Daniels and Deablo (a lock in the starting lineup), the Falcons would have two…

full_text:
Tyler Loop missed two 50-plus-yard field goals in the Ravens' preseason game against the Commanders Friday night. Tommy Gilligan / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Saturday’s NFL preseason action.
BALTIMORE — Now, the decisions begin.
The Baltimore Ravens wrapped up a dominant preseason with a 41-3 win over the Washington Commanders Friday night at M&T Bank Stadium. In going 3-0 in the preseason, Jesse Minter’s team outscored the opposition 78-13.
Minter kept most of his starters, and even some top backups, on the sideline throughout the preseason, so the team’s performance is a strong endorsement of its depth. That inevitably leads to tough decisions for general manager Eric DeCosta.
The Ravens have to cut their roster down to 53 by Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. They then will bring back many of the players they cut to their practice squad if they clear waivers. Practice squads will start forming Monday.
The uncertain health statuses of defensive end Nnamdi Madubuike, inside linebacker Teddye Buchanan and cornerback Bilhal Kone add a layer of difficulty in projecting the 53-man roster, but here’s our attempt to do just that.
In: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley
Out: Joe Fagnano, Austin Reed
Toughest call: Waiving Fagnano in hopes he’ll clear and return to the practice squad
It’s been treated like a foregone conclusion throughout the offseason that the Ravens would go with just two quarterbacks on the 53-man roster. That still could be their direction. The team’s decision-makers have repeatedly shown that they don’t place much value on rostering a third quarterback.
Still, the undrafted rookie out of UConn has forced them to make a difficult call. He’s played with poise and made some impressive throws and decisions. He certainly looks like a developmental quarterback a team would want to keep around. Fagnano played well enough that Baltimore can’t be too comfortable about the prospects of him clearing waivers, either.
In: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali, Adam Randall
Out: Elijah Tau-Tolliver, Jonathan Ward, Dontae McMillan
Toughest call: Keeping four backs rather than a third quarterback
There isn’t much ambiguity in the roster decisions on offense, but this is an area that could go either way. Neither Ali nor Randall has done enough to separate themselves as the clear winner of the No. 3 job, and Ali missed a lot of time with an undisclosed injury this summer.
The No. 3 back is expected to influence special teams far more than the offense, so that could give an edge to Ali, who played 55 percent of the team’s special teams snaps last year. However, the Ravens do not like cutting mid-round rookie draft picks, and Randall, a fifth-rounder, was owner Steve Bisciotti’s handpicked selection. That’s why it’s easy to foresee a scenario where both Ali and Randall make it.
In: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Ja’Kobi Lane, Devontez Walker, Elijah Sarratt, LaJohntay Wester
Out: Chris Moore, Xavier Guillory, Dayton Wade, Cornelius Johnson, Octavian Smith Jr., Cortez Braham Jr.
Toughest call: Deciding which two or three receivers to keep on the practice squad
The top five were all but set when training camp began a month ago, and Wester, as the team’s top punt returner, seemed close to a lock as long as he avoided ball-security issues during camp. He’s done that, and he’s shown promise as a wide receiver, too.
None of the other receivers really made much of a roster push, and Guillory, Wade and Smith battled injuries. Moore, given his experience and special teams ability, is probably a guy the Ravens would like to keep on the practice squad.
In: Mark Andrews, Durham Smythe, Matt Hibner, Josh Cuevas
Out: Ty Pezza, Lucas Scott (fullback)
Toughest call: Choosing between Hibner and Cuevas for the more prominent role
This is another position that’s been mostly set since before training camp started. The Ravens figure to rely heavily on tight ends in Declan Doyle’s offense and on special teams. With no true fullback being utilized, keeping four tight ends is hardly an imposition to the rest of the roster.
The only real decision will come on whether both Hibner and Cuevas can be active on game day, but the Ravens have time to sort that out.
In: Ronnie Stanley, John Simpson, Vega Ioane, Roger Rosengarten, Jovaughn Gwyn, Ethan Pocic, Carson Vinson, Emery Jones Jr., Andrew Vorhees
Out: Corey Bullock, David Sharpe, Evan Beerntsen, Gerad Lichtenhan, Diego Pounds, Nick Dawkins
Toughest call: Deciding who gets the ninth and final spot
The Ravens have gone with 10 offensive linemen before, but there’s not an obvious choice for that spot this year. Bullock missed so much time this summer, and Sharpe just signed about a week ago. Beerntsen, a rookie seventh-rounder, has played sparingly. Lichtenhan wasn’t able to build off a solid preseason opener.
Vorhees, the former starter at left guard, struggled at times, too. But his spot felt relatively secure once he agreed to a contract alteration. It feels like Pinter going down cleared up any ambiguity.
In: Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, Broderick Washington Jr., John Jenkins, Aeneas Peebles
Out: C.J. Okoye, Rayshaun Benny, David Olajiga, Dion Wilson Jr., Aaron Graves
Toughest call: Putting Madubuike on the active roster or starting him on injured reserve to give him another month-plus to clear mental and physical hurdles
Minter wasn’t definitive about whether Madubuike, who hasn’t progressed to team drills yet, will be ready for Week 1. The Ravens and Madubuike have been taking it extremely slow in his return from a neck injury. If the Ravens feel he still needs a few more weeks or even if he’ll be in a part-time role early in the season, it sure makes sense to keep an extra defensive lineman. They have also talked about limiting Campbell’s snaps early.
Peebles should have the edge on Okoye and Benny for the last spot, because his interior pass-rush ability adds diversity to the group. However, Peebles playing late in the final preseason game did feel ominous.
In: Trey Hendrickson, Tavius Robinson, Mike Green, Zion Young, Adisa Isaac
Out: Ethan Burke, Kaimon Rucker
Toughest call: Deciding whether to go with Isaac, Burke or Rucker for that fifth spot
The Ravens’ top four are set, and they’d probably be comfortable going into the season with just Hendrickson, Robinson, Green and Young on the 53. Yet, it’s always difficult for them to move on from an early-to-mid-round pick, and Isaac is a 2024 third-rounder who just hasn’t had a chance to develop because of injuries. It wouldn’t be surprising if the Ravens find a way to keep him and buy a little more time.
An undrafted free agent out of Texas, Burke has outplayed Isaac this summer and made a clear case. But he’s probably more likely to clear waivers than Isaac, and Day 2 draft picks get more time than undrafted free agents.
In: Roquan Smith, Trenton Simpson, Teddye Buchanan, Jay Higgins IV
Out: Carl Jones Jr. (IR candidate), Dominic DeLuca, Jamon Johnson, Michael Barrett
Toughest call: Determining whether Buchanan is close enough to game action to start him on the 53
Injuries have wreaked havoc on this position group and probably simplified decisions. Carl Jones, for one, was viewed as a strong candidate for the No. 4 inside linebacker/core special-teamer role, but he’s been out since early in camp. Jamon Johnson was a late signing, but a thumb injury took him out of the mix.
Higgins, a second-year undrafted free agent, has had a solid camp and appears to have the inside track for the No. 4 inside linebacker spot. However, DeLuca has opened up some eyes this summer as a rookie free agent and made the most of his preseason starter reps.
In: Marlon Humphrey, Nate Wiggins, Chidobe Awuzie, T.J. Tampa, Keyon Martin, Chandler Rivers
Out: Bilhal Kone (possible IR), Robert Longerbeam, Marquise Robinson, Amani Oruwariye, Lardarius Webb Jr.
Toughest call: Moving on from both Kone and Longerbeam
This is, by far, the most difficult position to whittle down. Kone and…

full_text:
Carolina's Trevis Gipson sacks Houston QB Davis Mills on Friday. Did Gipson's performance earn him a spot on the 53-man roster? Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — His team had just dispatched the Houston Texans in Friday’s preseason finale when Dave Canales’ thoughts quickly turned to the roster math facing the Carolina Panthers’ decision-makers this weekend.
Asked about rookie quarterback Haynes King, who had a terrific debut in the Hall of Fame Game but then missed the next three with a hamstring injury, Canales started working through the numbers at quarterback — and several other offensive positions.
“(Quarterback is) another decision. You talk about (running back) AJ Dillon, who had a great camp. Do you keep three quarterbacks? Four running backs?” Canales said. “How do you keep all these numbers — seven receivers, eight receivers that we’re talking about? The loaded tight end room of guys that we trust.
“So yeah, we got our work cut out for us in the next couple days.”
That work will start in earnest Saturday, when the Panthers’ first wave of early cuts is expected before Sunday’s 6 p.m. deadline to take rosters from 90 to 53 players.
Canales is right: This year’s roster projection was tricky business. But we’re rolling out one more version before the cuts start coming.
Changes from last week’s projection are noted in bold.
On: Bryce Young, Kenny Pickett, Haynes King
The last time we saw King, the undrafted free agent from Georgia Tech was making plays with his arm and legs in a win over the Arizona Cardinals in the Hall of Fame Game. Then he strained his hamstring diving into the end zone and aggravated it in the celebration that ensued. That left only August game tape for other teams to dig into — plus another 46 over King’s six college seasons. King said he believes he could have played Friday, but the team held him so the injury doesn’t nag him all season. He said the Panthers have given him no indication whether he’ll stick around. Asked if he thinks he could be claimed by another team, King said: “I’m not really looking into that. I love it here. … It feels like home.” One option: Teams can put up to two players on injured reserve before cuts and designate them to return, but they must sit out at least four games.
On: Chuba Hubbard, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne, AJ Dillon
After Hubbard returned too quickly from a calf injury last season, the team has taken a cautious approach with his hamstring strain so he can be 100 percent for Week 1. Brooks has looked strong in his return from a second ACL surgery, and his catch in a scramble situation was one of the few highlights for the first-team offense in the joint practice Wednesday with Houston. Etienne left Friday’s game after the first series with an ankle injury that will require imaging. Dillon had nine touches against the Texans, but averaged only 2 yards a carry.
On: Tommy Tremble, Ja’Tavion Sanders, Mitchell Evans, Feleipe Franks
Notable cut: Darren Waller
The Panthers signed Waller to a one-year deal for the veteran minimum of $1.3 million because they wanted to add competition to the tight end room. They also gave themselves options. If Waller is on the active roster for the first regular-season game, his deal becomes fully guaranteed. So they could choose to keep him on the practice squad initially, though they’d risk losing him to any interested team. General manager Dan Morgan could try to move Sanders, who’s been the subject of trade rumors.
Asked about Waller’s roster prospects, Canales said: “It’s certainly Dan and I looking at how we’re gonna use him and how he fits into the whole picture. And then of course it’s Darren, it’s his representation, making sure this is the right situation. And right now they feel like it is. But again those conversations have to happen and we’ll be making that decision in the next couple days.”
On: Tetairoa McMillan, Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Brycen Tremayne, Jimmy Horn, Ja’seem Reed
Injured reserve: Chris Brazzell, Dan Chisena
Notable cuts: David Moore, John Metchie, Casey Washington
Canales pointed to the receiver room as one of the strongest competitions. Horn played his way onto the roster with a strong finish in camp, including an eye-opening performance at Jacksonville when he made impact plays in the pass, run and return games. Moore has long been a favorite of Canales, but it feels like the final spot will come down to Metchie and Reed, who caught two passes for 37 yards Friday after missing the Jags game with a calf injury. Reed is younger and taller than Metchie, and can play more WR spots. Metchie has return ability. Tough call.
On: Rasheed Walker, Monroe Freeling, Robert Hunt, Damien Lewis, Luke Fortner, Sam Hecht, Brady Christensen, Stone Forsythe, Albert Reese
NFI/PUP lists: Taylor Moton, Ikem Ekwonu
Notable cut: Chandler Zavala, Jake Curhan
Freeling had a day to forget in the joint practice against the Texans, allowing at least four of the seven sacks Houston had on Young. The first-round pick from Georgia was overmatched against Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson. But with Moton and Ekwonu out indefinitely, the Panthers will take their lumps with Freeling as he tries to expedite his learning curve. I don’t have a great sense of what Morgan will do with the last OL spot or two. Reese was one of Pro Football Focus’ highest-rated rookies entering play Friday, but allowed a sack and four pressures against the Texans. But 6-foot-7, 325-pound dudes don’t grow on trees.
On: Derrick Brown, Bobby Brown, Lee Hunter, Cam Jackson, Jared Harrison-Hunte
PUP list: Tershawn Wharton
Canales wants to get both Derrick Brown and Bobby Brown a little more work during what amounts to a bye week after both missed time in camp with injuries. That gave young players like Hunter, the second-round pick from Texas Tech, Harrison-Hunte and Hall opportunities to show what they could do. This group still feels a little thin depth-wise, so don’t be surprised if Morgan tries to add to it. But it helps to have a Pro Bowler anchoring things. “It starts with the trenches,” Derrick Brown said this week. “Whoever wins the line of scrimmage wins the game. We know that.”
On: Jaelan Phillips, Patrick Jones, Princely Umanmielen, Trevis Gipson, Thomas Incoom
Notable cuts: Cam Gill, Jeremiah Moon
I had Gipson as one of the last cuts last week. But the 6-4, 264-pound Gipson made more plays than Gill as camp came to a close. The 29-year-old was active early against the Texans, sacking Davis Mills on Houston’s first offensive possession and then pressuring him on Lathan Ransom’s interception the next series. Incoom had a tackle for loss Friday, but his real value is as a four-phase special teams player.
On: Devin Lloyd, Trevin Wallace, Claudin Cherelus, Bam Martin-Scott, Jackson Kuwatch
Notable cut: Maema Njongmeta
International Player Program exemption: Maz Mwansa
The competition between Wallace and Cherelus for the second starting spot has received a lot of attention this summer, arguably more than it deserves. Why? Because the Panthers are in nickel a lot under Ejiro Evero, who likes using three-safety looks with Lloyd the lone inside linebacker. Wallace’s first-quarter sack of Mills was an example of the blitzing ability that could separate him from Cherelus.
On: Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Chau Smith-Wade, Will Lee, Akayleb Evans
Notable cuts: Corey Thornton , Devonta Smith, Robert Rochell
Special teams will be the determining factor for the last couple of spots on the 53. And the Panthers view Evans as their best gunner. So we’re giving him the edge over Thornton, who has struggled in coverage throughout the preseason. Smith, the undrafted free agent from Notre Dame, had two pass breakups and a run stop in one defensive series in the first half. He probably won’t make the 53, but the Panthers would love to sneak him through waivers and sign him back to the practice squad.

title: Bengals' final 53-man projection after perfect 3-0 preseason Cincinnati still has a big question at swing tackle. A trade or Sunday's NFL roster cutdown on could offer the answer. Paul Dehner Jr. 12

full_text:
Veteran quarterback Josh Johnson might have played his way into being a trade chip with another strong performance in Cincinnati's preseason finale against the Eagles on Friday. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Saturday’s NFL preseason action.
The Cincinnati Bengals concluded the preseason with a 30-13 win against the Philadelphia Eagles on Friday. They finish 3-0 with the first perfect preseason since 2006.
Head coach Zac Taylor stated earlier in the week that anybody playing in the game shouldn’t feel comfortable about their role. The number of Bengals players watching in street clothes and hats showed how good the club feels about the state of its roster.
The hours before the final cutdown deadline of 6 p.m. ET on Sunday will be full of tough decisions, how to stash prospects at particularly deep positions and the possibility of making a trade to solidify depth at tackle.
Just last year, the Bengals were desperate to add help in the trenches on both sides of the ball, and those needs were glaring during the miserable first half of the year. This year, the quality and depth across the roster, but particularly on the defensive line, have been a theme of the month. It will be an interesting spot to watch this weekend for that reason.
Coming out of Friday’s win, here’s a look at where each position stands ahead of the final cut, including practice squad priorities and potential to trade or utilize the waiver wire for outside additions.
Starter: Joe Burrow Backup: Joe Flacco Practice squad priority: Josh Johnson Cuts: Sean Clifford Trade or waiver wire? Could Johnson be traded?
Analysis: Simple and clear-cut here. Burrow and Flacco comprise arguably the best quarterback room in the NFL. Clifford more fits the developmental practice squad mold for a third quarterback and seems the natural fit there. But would a team with a shaky backup situation make a call about Johnson? He’s played for just about everyone in the NFL and showed again this preseason that he still has something to offer. More than likely, teams will wait for the Bengals to cut him, but with desperation at this position in the NFL, you never know for sure.
Friday impact: Another quality performance for Johnson, who went 12 of 19 for 156 yards playing in the first half. His control of the offense this preseason was impressive.
Starter: Chase Brown Backups: Samaje Perine, Tahj Brooks Practice squad priority: Kendall Milton Cuts: Gary Brightwell, Jamal Haynes, Kentrell Bullock Trade or waiver wire? Likely neither.
Analysis: Brooks endured two drops in the preseason, but he hasn’t been noted for those throughout camp. He hasn’t shown much explosiveness as a runner this preseason. Perine continues to be the ideal passing-down back and will hold down the backup gig.
Friday impact: Tough scene for the running backs. Brightwell, Bullock and Brooks (on kickoff return) lost fumbles. Brooks also failed to look dynamic as a runner once again. He logged six carries for 22 yards with a long of 10 through a big hole. It’s fair to wonder how the interested personnel department will be in cuts from other teams at running back. Meanwhile, in Haynes’ first real action of the preseason, he looked great, including a ridiculous 39-yard touchdown run to finish off the scoring.
Starters: Ja’Marr Chase, Tee Higgins, Andrei Iosivas Backups: Dohnte Meyers, Colbie Young, Charlie Jones Practice squad priority: Ke’Shawn Williams, Mitch Tinsley, Noah Thomas Cuts: Xavier Johnson, Jordan Moore, Kendric Pryor Trade or waiver wire? Would Charlie Jones fetch a player?
Analysis: Five locks here, including Meyers, who earned not just a roster spot but also a role in the offense. The question becomes who sticks in the final spot among Tinsley, Jones and Williams. The decision probably comes down to who is most likely to get poached off the practice squad. The Bengals would love to keep all of them. What they don’t want is a repeat of last year when they tried to stash Isaiah Williams on the practice squad and the Jets took him, forcing Cincinnati to search the waiver wire for an answer when Jones got hurt. Isaiah Williams ended up being named the Jets’ team MVP. Tinsley didn’t post a spectacular camp after opening eyes last year, but there’s still confidence in what he brings. How the front office executes this spot and potential roster gymnastics will be among the most interesting cutdown decisions.
Friday impact: Charlie Jones was returning punts during the first half, receiving three punts and gaining 39 yards. That suggests the Bengals view Jones as the returner. Meanwhile, Meyers continued to flex his muscles as a receiver. He caught three passes for 51 yards in the first drive, separating on all three levels. He will have a role in the offense on opening day.
Starters: Drew Sample, Mike Gesicki Backup: Erick All Jr., Tanner Hudson, Jack Endries Practice squad priority: Cam Grandy Cuts: Josh Kattus Trade or waiver wire? What could Hudson fetch?
Analysis: This position is directly impacted by the Bengals’ style-of-play decisions after the offseason of under-center exploration. A desire to run more 12 and 13 personnel from under center to close games would dictate a lean into extra blocking tight ends. Sample, Gesicki and All are locks. It’s extremely unlikely they cut seventh-round pick Endries. That leaves Grandy and Hudson. Could the Bengals use Hudson as a trade chip to fix the swing tackle spot? His production would be enticing for a team in need of a tight end. Then Grandy would eventually slip into the final spot.
Friday impact: Endries went down in the third quarter and retreated to the locker room with trainers, but returned. The fact that Hudson didn’t participate in this game makes sense, as the Bengals don’t need to see more of what he can do.
Starters: LT Orlando Brown, LG Dylan Fairchild, C Ted Karras, RG Dalton Risner, RT Amarius Mims Backups: C Connor Lew, OG Brian Parker II, OL Jalen Rivers, OT Javon Foster Practice squad priority: IOL Jacob Bayer Cuts: Andrew Coker, Corey Robinson II, Liam Brown, Christian Jones Trade or waiver wire? Looking to add at swing tackle
Analysis: The starters are locked in, and the young core of Lew, Parker and Rivers are as well. The swing tackle spot will be the one to watch over the next week. For now, Foster looks to be first off the bench if Mims or Brown gets hurt. The Bengals could attempt to acquire a tackle via trade or the waiver wire, with a trade for a veteran the most likely scenario. How confident the Bengals are in Lew’s knee opens the door for Bayer to step up early in the season, but otherwise, the interior depth spots are in good shape.
Friday impact: Taylor praised the offensive line after the game. Foster took a few rough pass-rush reps at left tackle. They weren’t the type of moments that win a job. The Bengals really need to be looking to deal for a veteran swing tackle. Lew playing 33 snaps was important, showing he’s prepared to play a full game as a backup if called upon.
Starters: Myles Murphy, BJ Hill, Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe Backups: Cashius Howell, Landon Robinson, TJ Slaton, Kris Jenkins, Cedric Johnson IR-return: Shemar Stewart Practice squad priority: Isaiah Foskey Cuts: McKinnley Jackson, Howard Cross III, Jordan Jefferson, Antwaun Powell-Ryland Trade or waiver wire? Could Jenkins be dealt?
Analysis: The epitome of good problems on the defensive line. Cincinnati shifted to a heavy dose of five-down-linemen base defense this year, which opens the possibility of keeping 11 from this group and only four linebackers. Stewart’s timeline is the variable here. He could be an IR-return candidate and come back from his hyperextended knee in Week 5 (Oct. 11). There’s a possibility to use Jenkins as a trade chip considering the Bengals have been successfully playing Slaton next to Lawrence in base situations and Stewart will occupy a versatile inside-outside spot when he returns. It feels like they’ll keep 10…

full_text:
What was Dae’Quan Wright before he became a professional with the Cleveland Browns? The answer to that question hovers over all of college athletics. Justin Ford / Getty Images
Dae’Quan Wright was on the field warming up with the Cleveland Browns before their preseason game last weekend. Three days later, he cleared NFL waivers with plans to return to college and play for LSU.
Then the SEC essentially told him no .
The Big Ten, SEC, Big 12 and ACC all moved this week to prevent athletes who crossed into professional sports from returning to compete in their conferences. That makes perfect sense. The NFL should be the Rubicon.
Declare for the draft, sign an NFL contract and join an NFL roster, and your college career should be over.
The harder question: What was Dae’Quan Wright before he became a professional?
What, exactly, is a college athlete in 2026?
For generations, college athletes were amateurs. They weren’t paid, they weren’t represented by agents, they couldn’t profit from endorsements. They couldn’t freely shop their services to another school, and their universities certainly weren’t sharing millions of dollars in athletic revenue with them.
Those restrictions supposedly separated college sports from professional sports.
They were also fundamentally dishonest.
College athletes generated billions while coaches earned millions, conferences signed massive television contracts and athletic departments built facilities resembling five-star resorts. Everyone surrounding the enterprise could maximize their economic value except the athletes creating the product. That system deserved to die.
College athletes can now earn NIL money, retain representation and transfer in search of better opportunities. Under the House v. NCAA settlement, schools can pay athletes directly through a new revenue-sharing system.
We have professionalized almost every economic component of major college sports. We just don’t call the athletes professional.
More importantly, universities don’t necessarily want to call them employees.
Calling athletes employees isn’t merely changing a noun. It potentially changes the balance of power. Employees may have rights under wage-and-hour laws and, depending on the applicable labor law, avenues to organize and collectively bargain over compensation and working conditions.
College sports have already conceded millions of dollars.
What it doesn’t want to concede is control.
In Johnson v. NCAA, a group of Division I athletes sued seeking minimum-wage compensation for the time they spent participating in their sports. The NCAA argued, in part, that college athletes were amateurs and therefore could not be employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
A federal appeals court rejected that premise.
The Third Circuit did not rule that every college athlete is an employee. It ruled that athletes can be employees depending on the actual economic relationship. It also stated that courts should examine whether an athlete performs services primarily for another party’s benefit, under that party’s control, in exchange for compensation or other benefits.
In other words, don’t tell us what you call them; show us what they actually do. The case isn’t finished. The appeals court merely ruled that college athletes could be employees and sent the case back to the trial court to determine whether they actually are.
So what is a college athlete? It’s quite literally a question a federal court still has to answer.
That’s what makes Wright’s bizarre trip from college to Cleveland and potentially back again so fascinating.
Everyone knew Wright became a professional when he signed an NFL contract.
What was he the day before?
He wasn’t an amateur in any traditional sense. He could be compensated. He could have representation. His economic value mattered.
Yet a system built around the revenue his athletic performance helps produce also stops short of calling him an employee.
As recently as January 2025, NCAA president Charlie Baker listed federal legislation affirming that college athletes are not employees among the NCAA’s three priorities in Congress.
That tells you how important the distinction is.
College sports spent a century insisting there were two categories — amateur and professional.
Then courts, athletes and basic economic fairness helped destroy the first category without universities being willing to fully embrace the second.
So what’s emerged in between?
Something college sports is still trying to define.
A college athlete can increasingly be compensated like a professional, represented like a professional and make economic decisions like a professional while participating in a system that insists none of those things necessarily makes him an employee.
But then what exactly is the relationship?
Wright’s specific eligibility dispute won’t answer that question. His case is unusual because he and other athletes from the high school Class of 2022 were told their college eligibility was exhausted, pursued professional opportunities and then won temporary relief from courts that reopened the possibility of another college season. That problem will eventually disappear.
The Class of 2022 will cycle through. New eligibility rules will solidify. The Power 4 conferences have made clear that athletes who cross into professional sports can’t simply return, so there won’t be a parade of second-year NFL players transferring back to Alabama or Ohio State.
But the larger question Wright exposed isn’t going anywhere.
What exactly are universities paying athletes for now?
If schools are sharing millions of dollars with athletes in a system created from athletic revenue, what is the nature of that payment? If the athlete isn’t an employee, what exactly is his relationship with the institution paying him?
And if he is performing a service that produces enormous value while operating under extensive rules governing where, when and how he performs it, at what point does the label “student-athlete” stop answering the economic question?
That’s why the wording matters.
For decades, “college athlete” meant amateur. That word no longer works.
Calling athletes professionals creates a distinction college sports desperately wants to preserve between Saturdays at LSU and Sundays with the Browns.
Calling them employees creates legal rights, obligations and bargaining power universities have spent years trying to avoid.
So college sports has created something in between.
Last Saturday, there was no ambiguity about Wright. He put on a Cleveland Browns uniform, and everyone agreed he was a professional football player.
The more revealing question is what everyone would have called him before that.
Amateur no longer fits, and professional apparently goes too far. “Employee” remains an ongoing legal fight.
College sports have changed almost everything about what its athletes can earn and how they can operate.
It still hasn’t figured out what, exactly, to call the people doing the work.

title: Cowboys 53-man roster projection: Will they keep 3 QBs? Which spots still need help? Jerry Jones said after the Cowboys' final preseason game that they would be "very, very aggressively" looking at upgrading the roster. Jon Machota 2

full_text:
Sam Howell had a strong outing Friday against the Saints. Could the Cowboys keep him and Joe Milton? Jerome Miron / Imagn Images
ARLINGTON, Texas — Jerry Jones said at the beginning of training camp that the Dallas Cowboys were open to making a “substantive” move if one was available. Since that time, their only notable move was signing veteran edge rusher Von Miller. But they’ve also been very fortunate in the health department.
Does that mean they are set, their final 53 being what they already have in the building?
“These could be some critical days here as we look at our roster, look at all the other rosters,” Jones said Friday night after Dallas’ final preseason game. “Right now, everybody around the league, the other 31 teams are seeing if they can improve it. We’ll be looking at that very, very aggressively. We’ve got time to improve for opening day.”
As the roster cuts become available on Sunday, it’s important to remember the Cowboys will have an excellent chance of getting most of the players they want back on their practice squad. Over the last five years, only four players the Cowboys have cut have been claimed by another team the following day: OLB Isaiah Land (Colts) in 2023, CB Eric Scott (Chiefs) and S Julius Wood (Titans) in 2024 and OLB Tyrus Wheat (Lions) last year.
“I think as a coaching staff, these next 24 hours-plus, we do focus on our own roster,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said, “and our guys, the guys that we know, the guys that we love, the guys that we care about, the guys that I’ve gotten to know their families, that I’ve gotten to know what motivates them, why they play this game.
“The personnel guys and the scouts, they’re diving into potential other roster moves. And that’s part of the business. We’ve got some time, but we have to make sure we get the decisions right, which we will, about our roster first. Then, of course, we handle it the right way with the guys that we love and care about.”
Based on three preseason games and 15 training camp practices, including one with the Rams and one with the Saints, here is our final 53-man roster projection.
Dak Prescott Joe Milton Sam Howell
Before Friday night’s preseason finale, it was only Prescott and Milton. Howell did enough to make me think the Cowboys will now go with three. Schottenheimer said the backup job is “neck and neck.” Jones said, “That’s one where we may just split the difference and have two backup quarterbacks.” Milton has had the better overall training camp and first two preseason games, but Howell has more experience and was the better player Friday night.
Javonte Williams Malik Davis Jaydon Blue Hunter Luepke
This is a solid running back room, but there would be concerns if they were without Williams for an extended period. Davis and Blue are good complements, but neither appears to be a lead back. Luepke gives Dallas help as a runner, blocker and receiver who can also play some tight end.
Jake Ferguson Brevyn Spann-Ford Luke Schoonmaker
Michael Trigg was a possibility with a strong training camp and preseason, but a toe injury limited him at times. He’d be an ideal candidate to return to the practice squad. Many outside the building have wanted to get rid of Schoonmaker. Many on the inside feel differently. Schoonmaker was one of the 34 players not wearing pads Friday night, usually a sign the player has already made the roster. Ferguson and Spann-Ford should be a very good one-two punch.
CeeDee Lamb George Pickens Ryan Flournoy KaVontae Turpin Jonathan Mingo Camden Brown
This is arguably the deepest wide receiver room in the NFL. They’d probably prefer to keep only five, but Brown and Mingo have played too well to cut. Mingo was another notable player not wearing pads Friday. Lamb, Pickens and Flournoy have a chance to be the first trio of wide receivers to all go over 1,000 yards since Larry Fitzgerald, Anquan Boldin and Steve Breaston did it with the Arizona Cardinals in 2008. That team went to the Super Bowl.
Tyler Smith, LG Tyler Booker, RG Cooper Beebe, C Tyler Guyton, LT Terence Steele, RT T.J. Bass, G Nick Leverett, G/C Trevor Keegan, G Nate Thomas, T Drew Shelton, T
The depth hasn’t looked very good all training camp. The Cowboys have their starting five and then Bass as their top reserve. After that, it’s all up in the air. Thomas could be the swing tackle, but if Guyton or Steele get injured, the next move could involve Smith moving out to tackle and Bass stepping in at left guard. Schottenheimer said Smith did not get any reps at left tackle during training camp because Guyton has “played as good of football as I’ve seen him play since he’s been a Dallas Cowboy.” This could be an area where they keep only eight or nine and look to add a veteran or two for depth from another team.
Quinnen Williams Kenny Clark Otito Ogbonnia Jonathan Bullard LT Overton
This is the best group of interior defensive linemen the Cowboys have had in a long time. Williams and Clark anchor everything, but the depth has a chance to be pretty good, too. They could keep a sixth, but this five seems like the most likely scenario. Williams, Clark, Ogbonnia and Bullard all were without pads Friday on the sideline.
Rashan Gary Donovan Ezeiruaku Von Miller Malachi Lawrence James Houston
The top four will see the bulk of the snaps as long as they’re healthy. Houston has proven he can get to the passer. Marist Liufau was going to be the sixth because of the help he brings on special teams, but he suffered a fractured left forearm Friday night that will require surgery.
“Losing Marist as a football player is tough,” Schottenheimer said. “Unfortunately, it’s part of the business. You guys all know him and the way he’ll attack his rehab. So, we’ll get surgery done as soon as we can and next man up. But yeah, he was a critical, critical part of not just two or three special teams, really all four. He’s a four-core guy that you just rely on and he plays the game with violence. We have some other guys in that locker room that do that as well.”
DeMarvion Overshown Dee Winters Jaishawn Barham Shemar James Justin Barron
This position group was the biggest question entering the draft. They then drafted Barham in the third round and traded for Winters. If all are healthy, this group could get the job done. But given the Cowboys’ luck at keeping top off-the-ball linebackers healthy, this could still be an area where another veteran is needed.
Daron Bland Shavon Revel Cobie Durant Devin Moore
Four is not enough. They probably need to add another player, either by claiming off waivers from another team’s cuts or by making a trade. Signing a veteran like Adoree’ Jackson could also be a possibility. The top three have looked good in camp. There wasn’t enough consistency to say anyone definitively grabbed the No. 4 spot. It’s likely multiple corners they cut will get back to their practice squad.
Caleb Downs Jalen Thompson Malik Hooker P.J. Locke Markquese Bell
Like their interior defensive line, the Cowboys have made significant upgrades at safety. The top four have all shown they can be counted on when the games matter. Downs will get a lot of work as the nickel cornerback, but he’ll also see plenty of reps at safety. This area has gone from what was one of Dallas’ biggest weaknesses to one of its greatest strengths.
Brandon Aubrey, K Bryan Anger, P Trent Sieg, LS
Not much projecting needed here. These are the only three at their positions. “I think I probably have the best group of specialists in the league,” Cowboys special teams coordinator Nick Sorensen said recently. “I’ve been fortunate. Same thing I felt last year with all three of them. It’s incredible. They’re really close, they’re really smart, and they’re pros. They do everything that makes it a lot easier for me.”

title: Broncos 53-man roster projection: Who grabs final spots at LB, TE? There could be heavy numbers on the defensive and offensive lines as Denver crafts a roster with title aspirations. Nick Kosmider 6

The Denver Broncos concluded their preseason Friday with a 34-6 victory over the Minnesota Vikings. Denver sat most of its starters and key reserves — roughly 30 players total — during the final dress rehearsal before the Sept. 14 opener at Kansas City.

full_text:
Broncos players made their final case to make the roster during Friday night's game against the Vikings. Ron Chenoy / Imagn Images
The Denver Broncos concluded their preseason Friday with a 34-6 victory over the Minnesota Vikings. Denver sat most of its starters and key reserves — roughly 30 players total — during the final dress rehearsal before the Sept. 14 opener at Kansas City.
Despite bringing back the bulk of a team that won 14 games last season and fell just short of a trip to the Super Bowl, head coach Sean Payton, general manager George Paton and their staff have a handful of interesting decisions to make as they put together an initial 53-man roster, which must be turned in by 4 p.m. MT Sunday.
Several factors could impact how the Broncos maneuver around the cuts with an eye on having not only the right players for the active roster, but also on the 16-man practice squad that can be assembled Monday. The Broncos are dealing with multiple injuries that could lead to short-term IR designations. Starting outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper could be facing an NFL suspension that Denver is also considering. Plus, Payton always seems to have a surprise or two when cuts arrive.
With all that in mind, let’s take one final crack at predicting where it will all land:
The Broncos cut Ehlinger at last season’s deadline, signed him to the practice squad and then moved him onto the 53-man roster ahead of Week 1 after an injury elsewhere on the roster opened a spot. There is a trust between the Broncos and Ehlinger, so it wouldn’t be surprising to see Denver handle the No. 3 quarterback spot in a similar fashion this season.
J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, Jonah Coleman
Others: Jaleel McLaughlin, Tyler Badie, Cody Schrader
The Broncos are facing tough choices at the back of this room. McLaughlin and Badie have both contributed to a team that has won 24 games over the past two seasons. Payton could decide he wants a pure runner on the roster, which would open a spot for McLaughlin. Or he could decide he needs a player well-versed in the position’s responsibilities in pass protection and hurry-up situations, which would give Badie the edge. The prediction here, though, is that Denver decides it has all it needs with its three top backs, reasoning that it could get at least one of Badie or McLaughlin through waivers and back to the practice squad.
A note here on fullback Adam Prentice: He will likely be on the game day roster every week this season so long as he is healthy, but the prediction here is he’ll be left off the initial 53-man roster in a procedural move that allows Denver to promote him from the practice squad the first three weeks of the season before moving him onto the roster for the rest of the season ahead of Week 4 — just as they did last year.
Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Marvin Mims, Pat Bryant, Troy Franklin
Others: Lil’Jordan Humphrey, Michael Bandy, Cameron Ross, Kyrese Rowan, Kolbe Katsis, Dane Key, Joseph Manjack, Kyre Duplessis
Regardless of how the roster is initially formed, Humphrey keeps managing to be a part of it. After returning to Denver midseason after a short stint with the New York Giants, the veteran had nine catches for 101 yards and a touchdown — and he added another scoring grab in the playoffs. Similar to the situation with Prentice, the Broncos could cut Humphrey and then move him to the roster via practice squad promotion. A wild card here is Ross. There probably isn’t room for the undrafted rookie on the roster, but he’s impressed during camp and has flexibility as a returner. He figures to be a player Denver would love to develop on the practice squad.
Evan Engram, Adam Trautman, Nate Adkins, Justin Joly
Others: Lucas Krull, Dallen Bentley, Caleb Lohner
Lohner, a seventh-round pick in 2025, seemed on track to compete for a roster spot in the spring, when Payton singled him out as a player who made a clear jump in his development since the end of last season. But Lohner has not participated in training camp while rehabbing an offseason injury. He began working on a side field during practice this week, but it’s hard to envision him being on the initial roster given his extended absence. Joly hasn’t convincingly outplayed Krull or Bentley in camp, but he was a fifth-round pick in April and Denver may have a tougher time getting him through waivers than the other two players we’re leaving off here. An 88-yard touchdown reception from Ehlinger in the fourth quarter Friday certainly didn’t hurt Joly’s case.
Garett Bolles, Ben Powers, Luke Wattenberg, Quinn Meinerz, Mike McGlinchey, Alex Palczewski, Kage Casey, Alex Forsyth, Matt Peart, Frank Crum
Others: Frank Crum, Tyler Miller, Lecitus Smith, Gavin Ortega, Reid Holskey, Calvin Throckmorton, Foster Sarell
Crum, who was the sixth lineman in jumbo sets for the Broncos during the second half of last season and caught a touchdown pass out of that personnel grouping against the Bills in the playoffs, is part of Denver’s plans on the offensive line. He’s also missed the past week of practice, which could signal a stay on injured reserve to start the season, but we won’t assume a long-term injury here since Payton hasn’t given a firm update on his status. Another roster candidate to watch here is Miller, the undrafted rookie out of Iowa State. You don’t find 6-foot-9, 335-pound offensive tackles around every corner, and Denver has made it a priority to keep developmental linemen when it can.
Zach Allen, D.J. Jones, Malcolm Roach, Eyioma Uwazurike, Tyler Onyedim, Jordan Jackson, Sai’vion Jones
Others: Jordan Miller, Kristian Williams, Israel Antwine
This may be the best and deepest position group on the team, and that’s reflected in the numbers here. Jackson has made the Broncos’ initial 53-man roster each of the past two seasons and may have turned in his best training camp yet. Sai’vion Jones, meanwhile, was a third-round pick just a year ago who produced an 11.5 percent pressure rate in three games played. The Broncos kept seven defensive linemen on the initial roster last season, and I see it shaking out that way again.
Nik Bonitto, Jonathon Cooper, Jonah Elliss, Que Robinson, Dondrea Tillman
Others: Drew Sanders, Ron Stone Jr., Dasan McCullough, Johnny Walker
Cooper was one of the only Broncos starters who played in Friday’s preseason finale. When he sees the field again remains an open question. The veteran is under investigation by the NFL after he was arrested twice in June following domestic incidents with his then-girlfriend. Cooper is facing multiple charges, including one for second-degree felony assault, and is scheduled to appear in court for an arraignment hearing Monday. Payton said earlier this week he believes the Broncos will “find out soon” whether the league will levy a suspension. Until there’s a concrete ban in place for Cooper, though, the Broncos will have a heavier number at this position. Still, it’s hard to see the group including Sanders, the fourth-year player who simply hasn’t been able to stay healthy.
Alex Singleton, Justin Strnad, Karene Reid, Red Murdock
Others: Jordan Turner, Taurean York
Reid made the initial 53-man roster as an undrafted rookie out of Utah last season and has called the defense for the second unit throughout the offseason. He also made one of Denver’s top defensive plays of the preseason when he broke on a short route in the red zone against the Falcons, deflecting a pass that was intercepted by Jahdae Barron and returned 97 yards for a touchdown. It would be a surprise if he were left off the roster. The decision here may be between Turner, the second-year player who saw action in seven games last season, and Murdock, the rookie taken by the Broncos with the final pick in April’s draft. I’m giving Murdock the edge, given his developmental upside.
Pat Surtain II, Riley Moss, Ja’Quan McMillian, Jahdae Barron, Kris Abrams-Draine
Others: Reese Taylor, Brent Austin, Sean Fresch Jr., Ricardo Hallman
It would not be a surprise…

Friday night might’ve been one of the most electrifying preseason games you’ll ever see. Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur certainly agrees.
“Was that not the most entertaining preseason game you’ve ever seen in your life?” he began his postgame news conference. “Eighty points!”
LaFleur and the Packers beat his little brother, Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur, 42-38, and now it’s time for the chopping block.
Rosters must be trimmed to 53 players by 5 p.m. CT on Sunday. Here’s one final projection of what that group will look like.
Quarterback (2): Jordan Love, Tyrod Taylor
The social media streets are probably rampant with calls for McCord to pass Taylor on the depth chart, but that’s not happening.
Two things can be true at once: McCord played quite well in preseason games, most notably his four-touchdown barrage on Friday night, and Taylor is better suited to back up Love.
It’s important to remember that NFL defenses are more vanilla than ice cream in the preseason. They’ll be far more complex when the games count.
Taylor, 37, has seen every look under the sun. He might not have McCord’s upside at this point, but he can operate an offense and help the Packers tread water if Love goes down. He’s probably the safer option, and that’s important.
Should McCord make it through to the practice squad, he can continue to develop there. The Packers haven’t kept three quarterbacks since 2020, when they kept Tim Boyle because Love wasn’t ready to back up Aaron Rodgers yet and they couldn’t release their first-round pick.
“We brought Tyrod in here for a reason, and we’re very happy we have him,” general manager Brian Gutekunst said on Wednesday.
Side note: LaFleur revealed that Love called plays in the second half against the Cardinals. The Packers scored 18 points in the fourth quarter and erased an 11-point deficit with less than five minutes remaining.
“A lot more calm,” LaFleur said of Love. “I think I learned something from him today.”
Running back (3): Josh Jacobs, MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks
Released: Pierre Strong Jr., Jaden Nixon, Damien Martinez
We’ll wait to see whether Jacobs is suspended before roster cutdown day or Week 1, if at all. The Brown County district attorney formally charged him with misdemeanor battery and criminal damage to property on Thursday. However, the NFL has yet to levy discipline, and the case is still ongoing.
If the league suspends him after cutdown day but before the season starts, the Packers will likely have Strong on the practice squad and can call him up if they don’t bring someone in from outside the building.
“You gotta let everything play out,” LaFleur said of Jacobs’ situation, “but I anticipate him being a member of our football team.”
Wide receiver (6): Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Matthew Golden, Skyy Moore, Savion Williams, Bo Melton
Released: J. Michael Sturdivant, Will Sheppard, Isaiah Neyor, Kaden Prather, Kisean Johnson, Chris Hilton Jr.
Sturdivant and Sheppard certainly made their cases for roster inclusion late in camp. Sturdivant, an undrafted rookie, caught six passes for 112 yards and a touchdown on Friday night, while Sheppard caught a touchdown for a second straight week and also returned a punt 81 yards for a score.
I’ve yet to be impressed by Williams in Green Bay, but he was a third-round pick last year and isn’t getting cut. Moore will be the team’s primary returner, and Melton is a jack-of-all-trades locker-room favorite.
I don’t think the Packers keep seven receivers, but Sturdivant and Sheppard both deserve a spot if they do. Sturdivant especially has opened eyes all camp, but many teams have skill players who flash in the summer. He probably has less of a chance to be claimed on waivers than you think.
“It’d be a dream come true,” Sturdivant said of potentially making the team. “You dream of making it to the NFL your whole life. Honestly, you put all the work in to make it happen, so it would be a great feeling. But it’s not the end goal. My dream wasn’t just to make the team for a day.”
Tight end (3): Tucker Kraft, Josh Whyle, Jonnu Smith
Released: Drake Dabney, Messiah Swinson, McCallan Castles, Thomas Yassmin
The arrival of Smith , the 31-year-old who played for LaFleur on the Tennessee Titans in 2018, means Dabney hits the road in this projection (the Packers have yet to announce Smith’s signing officially). They’d better pray to the heavens that Kraft doesn’t get hurt again, if only because what they have behind him is still quite underwhelming.
Offensive line (10): Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Jager Burton, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk, Anthony Belton, Zach Bako-Bewele, John Williams, Donovan Jennings, Travis Glover
Released: Darian Kinnard, Dalton Cooper, Dillon Wade, Dylan Barrett, Josh Gesky, Brant Banks
Kinnard was Green Bay’s swing tackle last season, but playing in the third quarter of the preseason finale as a veteran isn’t a good sign. The Packers might rather take a flier on the upside of Glover, who missed all of last season with an injury.
Interior defensive line (6): Devonte Wyatt, Karl Brooks, Javon Hargrave, Chris McClellan, Anthony Campbell, Jonathan Ford
Released: Nazir Stackhouse, Jaden Crumedy
I don’t know for certain that Brinson will land on injured reserve. It’s more of a guess because I needed to clear one spot on the 53, and I don’t think they take seven interior defensive linemen, but I couldn’t bring myself to cut Campbell or Ford after the preseasons they’ve had.
Brinson injured his calf warming up for the second preseason game and has been out since. LaFleur said “to be determined” Friday night when asked whether the currently injured trio of Brinson, Savion Williams and edge Collin Oliver could miss substantial time to begin the season.
“I feel like my odds are pretty high to make this team and contribute to this football club this year,” Ford said.
Edge (5): Lukas Van Ness, Brenton Cox Jr., Barryn Sorrell, Collin Oliver, Dani Dennis-Sutton
Released: Nyjalik Kelly, Aaron Mosby, Arden Walker
Kelly had a really nice preseason finale. There have been some “47” scribbles in my notebook this summer, too, because of standout plays from the undrafted rookie out of Central Florida in practice. Assuming he makes the practice squad, his potential is enticing.
If Oliver lands on IR, Kelly should make the 53. Dennis-Sutton, the rookie fourth-round pick, made his preseason debut Friday after missing two games with a heat-related illness and did so with a bang. With more time on task, he could crack the Parsons-less rotation.
Linebacker (5): Edgerrin Cooper, Zaire Franklin, Isaiah McDuffie, Ty’Ron Hopper, Nick Neimann
Released: Kristian Welch, TJ Quinn
This is a cut-and-dried group. There’s not much to see here.
Cornerback (6): Brandon Cisse, Keisean Nixon, Carrington Valentine, Benjamin St-Juste, Kamal Hadden, Domani Jackson
Released: Jaylin Simpson, MJ Devonshire Jr., Shemar Bartholomew
Jackson is a rookie sixth-round pick out of Alabama who missed time in camp while recovering from offseason core muscle surgery. He played poorly on Friday night, most notably missing a couple of tackles on the same drive and allowing a 41-yard touchdown on a deep corner route.
However, Gutekunst has only released two of his 12 sixth-round picks on roster cutdown day since becoming GM in 2018.
Safety (4): Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams, Javon Bullard, Kitan Oladapo
Released: Mark Perry, Murvin Kenion III, Tra Fluellen, Trey Dean III
Perry had some nice moments this summer, but he can be a game-day elevation if need be. Bullard, Oladapo and Hadden will be the team’s three slot defenders this season.
Special teams coordinator Cam Achord said he cares more about Smack’s kicks in stadiums than on the practice field. Good thing, too, because Smack had a rocky summer at Ray Nitschke Field but…

full_text:
Chiefs cornerback Kristian Fulton, breaking up a pass intended for Seahawks wide receiver Cody White, had his best preseason game Friday night. Jamie Squire/ Getty Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The Kansas City Chiefs’ 9-9 home tie against the Seattle Seahawks on Friday night was the last chance for players on the bubble to make their case for the 53-man roster.
Wide receiver Andrew Armstrong had his best game while serving as quarterback Garrett Nussmeier’s top target. Backup center Pete Nygra cleared holes in the run game, and veteran guard Mike Caliendo also impressed, making a final roster statement.
Will it be enough ahead of Sunday’s cutdowns? It’s time to peer into the crystal ball to reveal our official (and final) Chiefs 53-man roster projection.
In: Patrick Mahomes, Justin Fields, Garrett Nussmeier
Missed the cut: Chris Oladokun
The Chiefs have a good problem here: Nussmeier has shown enough growth in preseason that he’ll require a 53-man roster spot to be protected. He seems on a path to becoming Mahomes’ long-term backup in K.C.
In: Kenneth Walker III, Emmett Johnson, Emari Demercado, Brashard Smith
Missed the cut: Jaydn Ott, E.J. Smith
Each running back appears to have his own niche. Walker is the workhorse who’ll be asked to do more than he did in Seattle. Johnson would be next in line for primary work if Walker gets hurt, and he also should be a special teams staple. Demercado profiles as a third-down back and the room’s best pass protector, while Brashard Smith gives coach Andy Reid a gadget-type guy who can catch out of the backfield and is a potential red zone weapon. Again, keeping four instead of three here means there will need to be extra trimming at other positions.
In: Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, Jalen Royals, Cyrus Allen, Andrew Armstrong
Missed the cut: Nikko Remigio, Jimmy Holiday, Jason Brownlee, Xavier Loyd, Omari Evans, Jacob De Jesus, Jeff Weimer
Remigio remains a high-floor, low-ceiling option at returner, and it seems likely he’d get back to the practice squad. We say the Chiefs go that route here while believing Smith and Allen can handle punt returns for the short term, with the option to elevate Remigio later if things don’t go well. In this scenario, Armstrong claims one of the last roster spots as a taller red zone weapon while flashing as an excellent run blocker. Armstrong led the Chiefs with five catches for 54 yards in Friday’s game.
In: Travis Kelce, Noah Gray, Jared Wiley, Jake Briningstool
Missed the cut: Tre Watson, Mason Pline
Briningstool appeared to earn his way onto the roster with a strong finish near the end of training camp. Most importantly, he’s been able to stay on the field after sitting out last season with a hamstring injury. This group has no true run-blocking specialist at the moment. Could Wiley start to prove more capable? Or might Armstrong play a tight-end-type role in those scenarios?
In: Josh Simmons, Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey, Trey Smith, Jaylon Moore, Kahlil Benson, Esa Pole, Joshua Ezeudu, Hunter Nourzad
Missed the cut: Mike Caliendo, Pete Nygra, C.J. Hanson, Ethan Driskell, Chu Godrick, Josh Thompson
One would think the Chiefs’ trade this week for Ezeudu should push either Caliendo or Nourzad off the roster. The guess here is the Chiefs will keep the younger Nourzad — he’s a 2024 fifth-round pick — while still going relatively light with only nine O-line bodies. The last game will make for a tough evaluation, though. Based on preliminary Pro Football Focus analysis, Caliendo was the Chiefs’ top-graded offensive player Friday. Nygra also had an excellent showing in the preseason finale, so he has a chance of sneaking onto the 53 as well.
In: George Karlaftis, Chris Jones, Khyiris Tonga, Ashton Gillotte, Peter Woods, R Mason Thomas, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Emmanuel Ogbah, Marcus Harris
PUP list: Omarr Norman-Lott
Missed the cut: Tyreke Smith, V.J. Anthony, Amari McNeill, Cole Brevard, Damon Payne, Ethan Hurkett, Niles King
The Chiefs have gone with at least nine defensive linemen every year under Reid , meaning an under-the-radar player could slip into the rotation here if Norman-Lott starts the year on the physically unable to perform list while rehabbing a knee injury. We’ll give that spot to Harris, who joined the team late last year and appears to be next in line among defensive tackles. Harris helped his case Friday with a tackle for loss just after halftime and six tackles overall. The Chiefs also haven’t disclosed much about Gillotte’s foot injury, so he might be a candidate for injured reserve, which would keep him out the first four weeks.
In: Drue Tranquill, Nick Bolton, Cooper McDonald, Jeffrey Bassa, Jack Cochrane
Missed the cut: Cam Jones, Cole Christiansen, Kam Arnold, Wesley Bissainthe
Something to note: This is one spot where the Chiefs could play some roster tricks. Cochrane (like Ogbah and cornerback L’Jarius Sneed) is a vested veteran, meaning he could get “cut” Sunday only to return to the team or practice squad without having to pass through waivers. It would be a creative way for the Chiefs to pick up a roster spot, especially if a few unexpected players start the season on the PUP list.
In: Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, Chris Roland-Wallace, Jadon Canady, L’Jarius Sneed, Kristian Fulton
Missed the cut: Kader Kohou, Melvin Smith, Kevin Knowles, Kaiir Elam, Bryce Phillips, D’Arco Perkins-McAllister, Zelmar Vedder
The Chiefs could cut Fulton to save $5 million in salary-cap space (while eating $8 million in dead money), so it’s worth noting that Fulton had his best preseason game Friday with a pass breakup and strong coverage with the second-stringers. K.C. has not run him with the starters at any point in camp, so it still wouldn’t be surprising if he’s not with the team Sept. 14, whether that means he’s traded or cut. Smith and Knowles seem like practice squad candidates, while Kohou appeared to drop down the depth chart later in camp.
In: Alohi Gilman, Chamarri Conner, Jaden Hicks, Xavier Nwankpa
Missed the cut: DeShon Singleton, Tanner McCalister
Nwankpa should join Benson as the only two undrafted free agents to make the roster. He’s definitely the team’s fourth safety (or fifth if you count the versatile Roland-Wallace, who plays there too), but Nwankpa profiles as an excellent special-teamer right away and should be a top contributor there if he makes the cut.
In: K Harrison Butker, P Matt Araiza, LS James Winchester
No competition here, though Butker needs to show more consistency this season to avoid a camp battle in 2027.

full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa completed 7 of 8 passes for 95 yards for the Falcons in his preseason return to Miami. Carmen Mandato / Getty Images
Miami Dolphins fans greeted Tua Tagovailoa with boos Friday night in his return to the stadium he once called home.
But the Atlanta Falcons quarterback insisted that while he heard those boos, they didn’t taint his perspective on the place he spent the first six years of his NFL career.
“Those are probably some of the best six years of my life, being able to play for Miami, being able to play in front of the crowd,” Tagovailoa said after Friday night’s preseason finale between the Dolphins and Falcons at Hard Rock Stadium.
“… So, regardless of the reaction, I love the city. We have a home out here. We still have our house and whatnot, but I mean, it is what it is. I can’t change any of what they did and whatnot. But it was really cool to see a lot of the guys after the game and then talk to some of the guys during the game. It was a cool homecoming, if you will.”
The Dolphins released Tagovailoa in March, resulting in a record $99.2 million in dead money on Miami’s cap sheet two years after the franchise signed him to a contract extension that made him one of the highest-paid players in NFL history.
The Dolphins reached the playoffs twice in the six seasons after they selected Tagovailoa with the No. 5 pick in the 2020 NFL Draft. The Alabama product endured multiple head injuries during that time, and the team struggled over his final two seasons, going 15-19 as Tagovailoa started 25 of 34 games.
Not only did Tagovailoa’s play suffer in 2025, but he also made headlines for saying the wrong things , and he was eventually benched after the team’s 28-15 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 15.
“Obviously, it wasn’t fun being in my position,” Tagovailoa said. “But outside of that, I wasn’t playing up to the standard that I had been playing in years past, so I understand. You have to be real with yourself. That’s what it was, bottom line. Outside of that, with how things went after, with a trade or cutting me or whatnot, I think (coach Jeff) Hafley and (general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan), they were really, really good in that process with me.”
Tagovailoa, who is competing with Michael Penix Jr. for the starting job in Atlanta, fumbled a snap late in the first quarter that was recovered by the Dolphins. Aside from that, he put together a decent performance, completing 7 of 8 passes for 95 yards.
