full_text:
Is quarterback J.J. McCarthy's future in Minnesota in question following the team's final preseason game? Isaiah J. Downing / Imagn Images
The Minnesota Vikings concluded their preseason Friday night in Denver with a 34-6 loss to the Broncos . None of Minnesota’s starters played.
Perhaps the most significant development came in the first quarter, when undrafted free-agent safety Jacob Thomas rolled his ankle. He did not return. After the game, coach Kevin O’Connell said Thomas has an ankle sprain and will get an MRI this weekend. His diagnosis is important at a position already navigating multiple injuries.
Beyond that, NFL teams must evaluate their depth by Sunday afternoon. A flurry of activity is set to begin. Who are the likeliest players to make the Vikings’ 53-man roster? Here is our final projection:
In: Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz
Out: J.J. McCarthy, Max Brosmer
McCarthy’s rough week added further murkiness about his status for 2026. The 23-year-old exited the second preseason game with an ankle injury, then practiced Monday and Tuesday. O’Connell gave him the day off Wednesday so that he could rest up enough to start Friday’s final preseason matchup with the Broncos. But McCarthy did not play. Wentz started and appears to be in line to be the team’s backup. McCarthy’s comfort (or lack thereof) with being QB3 could dictate his future in Minnesota.
The Vikings value Brosmer’s smarts and knowledge of the system, but his lackluster preseason performance casts some doubt on his future, as well.
In: Aaron Jones, Jordan Mason, Demond Claiborne
Scott’s understanding of special teams complicates this choice. He also played 105 offensive snaps in 2025. The Vikings could slide him to the practice squad, a move that could open the door for a younger player with more developmental upside. Claiborne’s burst and explosiveness give him more time to learn O’Connell’s complex offensive scheme, but the Vikings are banking here on the health of Jones and Mason.
If the Vikings are committed to reshaping their offense to emulate what the Miami Dolphins have done in recent years, they’ll need Bredeson to shine. He has taken to the team’s system quickly. Minnesota’s attention to the fullback position is clear given they’ve also worked edge rusher Chaz Chambliss at the role in practice to cover for Bredeson, if need be.
In: Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison, Jauan Jennings, Tai Felton, Myles Price
Out: Dillon Bell, Jeshaun Jones, Terrill Davis, Dontae Fleming, Michael Briscoe, Trayvon Rudolph, Marcus Sanders Jr.
There isn’t much suspense here. Felton and Price established themselves as worthy backups if needed in a pinch.
Maybe the biggest source of curiosity here is how often the Vikings will use 11 personnel in 2026. Jennings’ blocking ability gives the team a different way to dictate matchups with the defense. Exposing Bell to waivers might pique another team’s interest, especially given that he was sought after in undrafted free agency.
In: T.J. Hockenson, Josh Oliver, Ben Yurosek, Gavin Bartholomew
Out: Marshall Lang, Matt Lauter
Tight end No. 3 remains one of the key roster pivot points. Yurosek is an admirable blocker with special teams experience, while Bartholomew catches passes with ease down the seams. Minnesota could roll with both. It could also explore the waiver wire for more veteran insurance.
Projecting the tight end situation behind Hockenson and Oliver is one of the toughest tests in this 53-man exercise.
In: Christian Darrisaw, Donovan Jackson, Blake Brandel, Will Fries, Brian O’Neill, Ryan Van Demark, Caleb Tiernan, Michael Jurgens, Joe Huber
Out: Walter Rouse, Vershon Lee, Joshua Gray, Tomas Rimac, Delby Lemieux, Gavin Gerhardt, Tristan Leigh
One of the underrated storylines of training camp? The health and commitment of the starting offensive line. Brandel’s snap exchanges are worth watching when the season begins, but the consistency of the primary five has been vital.
Injuries could leave the Vikings in a precarious position. Tiernan has a left ankle injury. Van Demark, Jurgens and Huber have all put both highs and lows on tape in the preseason. This is another area where the Vikings could look to add help.
In: Jalen Redmond, Levi Drake Rodriguez, Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins, Domonique Orange, Caleb Banks, Elijah Williams
Out: Isaiahh Loudermilk, Jahvaree Ritzie, Smith Vilbert, Jonathan Harris
Proceed with these six, and the Vikings will be finalizing a drastic year-over-year transition. In 2025, aging veterans Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave anchored the interior. Now, youth dominates the position.
Rodriguez is a key piece of the Vikings defense at nose tackle, while Ingram-Dawkins’ versatility allows for flexibility on the front. Orange looks closer to contributing than Banks. But Williams’ preseason output caught the attention of NFL evaluators. The Vikings recognize his impact.
In: Andrew Van Ginkel, Dallas Turner, free-agent signing, Tyler Batty, Bo Richter, Chaz Chambliss
Out: Kenny Dyson, Cam’Ron Stewart
Trading Jonathan Greenard to the Philadelphia Eagles allowed Turner to assume a starting role. Teammates raved about his growth after joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens. A breakout season could help Minnesota maintain its defensive standing near the top of the league.
Backups like Batty, Richter and Chambliss received praise from coaches. Still, the Vikings could benefit from a productive pass-rushing veteran behind Turner and Van Ginkel. Hence, the inclusion of a free-agent signing, which could happen in the coming week.
In: Blake Cashman, Eric Wilson, Jake Golday, Ivan Pace Jr.
Out: Jacob Roberts, Bangally Kamara, Josh Ross
Few Vikings performed better than Cashman throughout training camp. He intercepted a Lamar Jackson pass in joint practices with the Ravens. His comfort in defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ system is apparent. His partnership with Wilson matters with the safety spot in flux.
Behind those two, the Vikings have more options than in recent years. Golday impressed during training camp off the ball and on the edge. Pace’s ability to wreak havoc makes him a weapon. Roberts’ preseason showings are deserving of an opportunity. Minnesota will have to assess how willing it’d be to watch another team lure him away.
In: Byron Murphy Jr., Isaiah Rodgers, James Pierre, Charles Demmings
Out: Da’Veawn Armstead, Zemaiah Vaughn, Bryce Phillips, Jarod Washington, Tre Hawkins III, Marcus Allen
Minnesota improved its cornerback depth this offseason. Pierre provides more anticipatory ability than Jeff Okudah did last year, and Demmings is more athletic than former Viking Fabian Moreau. Depending on the complexion of the safety room, Flores could utilize Pierre or Demmings against three-receiver sets.
The team could also keep Armstead — an undrafted corner from North Texas — if it prefers a nickel body type with potential.
In: Josh Metellus, Theo Jackson, Jay Ward, Jacob Thomas, Jakobe Thomas, free-agent signing
Out: Tavierre Thomas, Kahlef Hailassie
This position group comes with questions. First and foremost, will the Vikings roster Tavierre Thomas, whose role is mostly on special teams? And second, do the other safeties offer enough reliability?
Tavierre Thomas only played 18 defensive snaps in 2025. Waiving him would require the Vikings to have a backup plan alongside receiver Tai Felton at gunner. But the possibility of choosing another offensive or defensive contributor could outweigh the gunner value.
Meanwhile, we included a free-agent signee amid the uncertainty surrounding franchise legend Harrison Smith. The 37-year-old has not made a final decision on his future. Minnesota might need him to return to maximize its chances on the back end.
In: Will Reichard (K), Andrew DePaola (LS), Brett Thorson (P)
There’s some intrigue at punter. The Vikings signed Hekker, who earned first-team All-Pro honors four times between 2013 and 2017, but his production dipped in recent years with the Panthers and Titans. That, paired with…

full_text:
New York Giants wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. caught three passes for 54 yards during Friday's game against the New York Jets. Yannick Peterhans / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Saturday’s NFL preseason action.
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Projecting 53-man rosters in the NFL has become more complicated with rules that allow for greater practice squad flexibility. Decisions aren’t made entirely based on assembling the best 53-player team, as there are considerations for which bubble players could be poached if they don’t make the roster.
There was an example of this dance last summer when the New York Giants initially kept rookie seventh-round pick Korie Black on their 53-man roster. Black was cut the next day after the Giants made waiver claims. The Giants planned to slide Black to their practice squad, but he instead elected to sign with the Jets’ practice squad (the Giants eventually signed him back to their active roster during the season).
It’s challenging to forecast these roster gymnastics when projecting a 53-man roster, but here’s my best shot at nailing down who will be on the Giants’ roster after Sunday’s 6 p.m. deadline for cuts:
In: Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston Out: Brandon Allen, Jake Haener
There’s no thought of keeping three quarterbacks. Winston is arguably the best backup in the league, which is especially valuable considering how many hits Dart takes. The Giants can sign Allen to the practice squad if they want to keep him in the quarterback room.
In: Cam Skattebo, Najee Harris, Devin Singletary, Tyrone Tracy Jr. Out: Eric Gray, Damon Bankston
Harris’ signing combined with Tracy’s high-profile preseason gaffes has caused a stir in the running back room. But it would be an overreaction to cut Tracy, especially with the limited upside of Harris and Singletary. Tracy looked explosive while carrying the ball four times for 37 yards and a touchdown in Friday’s preseason finale against the Jets. He left early to get evaluated for a concussion, but he was cleared. Coach John Harbaugh said after the game that Tracy had a stinger.
One of these running backs will likely be a healthy scratch on game day. Tracy’s role on special teams could help him avoid that fate.
In: Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, Darius Slayton, Braxton Berrios, Odell Beckham Jr. Out: Dalen Cambre, Isaiah Hodgins, Xavier Gipson, Jalin Hyatt, Kobe Prentice
Calvin Austin III’s torn ACL was a blow, but it cleared up the cloudy picture for the sixth wide receiver spot that was likely going to come down to Berrios vs. Beckham. Now, Berrios is a near lock to make it as Austin’s replacement as the top punt returner. Beckham should be safe as well, especially coming off his best week of camp. That carried over to three catches for 53 yards in Friday’s preseason finale.
It could come down to Beckham vs. Slayton for one jersey on game day. Cambre is a special teamer, but he hasn’t been starting on those units during camp. He’s an ideal player to stash on the practice squad.
Odell Beckham Jr.’s best week of camp has come this week, coach John Harbaugh said. #giants pic.twitter.com/n0BWHvGkiK
— Charlotte Carroll (@charlottecrrll) August 26, 2026
In: Isaiah Likely, Theo Johnson, Chris Manhertz, Pat Ricard Out: Thomas Fidone II, Tanner Conner, Grant Finley, Josiah Degaura
This is a crowded room since Ricard, a fullback, is grouped with the tight ends. Manhertz was voted to the team’s eight-man leadership committee and is valued for his blocking ability in what promises to be a run-heavy offense. The only question is how the Giants handle Fidone. He has flashed dynamic physical traits when healthy, so it would be risky to expose the 2025 seventh-round pick to waivers, especially with former coach Brian Daboll hoarding Giants players in Tennessee. This could be a situation where the Giants keep five tight ends initially to shield Fidone and then finagle the roster leading into the opener.
In: Andrew Thomas, Jon Runyan, John Michael Schmitz Jr., Francis Mauigoa, Jermaine Eluemunor, Marcus Mbow, Aaron Stinnie, Lucas Patrick, JC Davis Out: Bryan Hudson, Evan Neal, Jake Kubas, Brenden Jaimes, Ryan Schernecke, Jarrod Gray
The recent trades of Daniel Faalele and Josh Ezeudu cleared up the offensive line picture. The five starters are locked in, while Mbow and Stinnie will serve as the top backups. Davis is likely headed for a redshirt year as the fourth tackle after an impressive preseason. The battle between Patrick and Hudson for the backup center job is coming down to the wire.
Patrick replaced Schmitz on the Giants’ third drive in the preseason finale. Patrick played the rest of the first half before Hudson took over in the third quarter.
A case can be made for either player. Patrick’s experience (65 career starts) playing guard and center is an advantage. However, his “old knees,” as Harbaugh called them, had to be managed throughout the offseason. It would be concerning to rely on a 33-year-old with an injury history as the backup center, especially considering Schmitz has missed multiple games in each of his three seasons and was sidelined by a concussion this summer. Hudson is eight years younger, so he presents far more upside, but he lacks game experience.
There’s a scenario where the Giants keep Patrick and Hudson, but that feels like overkill. Center injuries around the league raise the odds of the loser of the competition getting scooped up. Patrick’s experience makes him a greater risk to be claimed, so I think the Giants will roll the dice on sliding Hudson through to the practice squad.
In: DJ Reader, Shelby Harris, Chauncey Golston, Darius Alexander, Bobby Jamison-Travis Out: Leki Fotu, Marlon Davidson, Zacch Pickens, Josh Tupou, Anquin Barnes Jr., Ben Barten
The Giants are banking on Reader and Harris to anchor the defensive line. There are concerns with the team managing the 35-year-old Harris’ reps throughout the summer. Dexter Lawrence played 754 snaps in the middle last season. Harris played 509 snaps, and Reader played 583, so even if the vets stay healthy, there are a lot of snaps that will be left to an uninspiring supporting cast.
Alexander’s struggles led to the 277-pound Golston sliding to defensive end from outside linebacker. Jamison-Travis isn’t ready to contribute now, but it could be risky to expose the sixth-round rookie to waivers. He’s a candidate for the aforementioned Black roster move, where he makes the initial 53-man roster and then is passed to the practice squad when an addition is made after cut day. It would be shocking if there isn’t a defensive lineman added before the opener, whether that’s via the waiver wire or a trade.
In: Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Caleb Murphy Out: Khalid Kareem, Trace Ford
Golston’s shift to the defensive line opened a spot at outside linebacker, and Murphy appears ready to seize it. He has moved into a core special teams role, which is crucial for backup linebackers seeking a roster spot.
In: Tremaine Edmunds, Arvell Reese, Micah McFadden, Jack Kelly, Zaire Barnes Out: Darius Muasau, Anfernee Orji, Chandler Martin
McFadden and Kelly will be core special teamers and quality backups at inside linebacker. Barnes has emerged as a core special teamer ahead of Muasau. The Giants could also carry Muasau, but that seems heavy at this position.
In: Greg Newsome II, Deonte Banks, Dru Phillips, Paulson Adebo, Colton Hood, Nic Jones Out: Korie Black, Art Green, Ugo Amadi, JT Woods
Newsome, Banks, Phillips, Adebo and Hood are locks, although the competition for the starting outside corner jobs continues. Jones, Green and Black all have a case for the final corner spot. Green is the most accomplished special teamer in that trio, but he has ceded first-team reps lately. He got hurt in the fourth quarter of the preseason finale, which could seal his fate. Black is the best corner of the group, but he hasn’t been a factor on special teams. Black pulled his groin in the preseason finale, which…

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The preseason is over for the New York Giants, which means it’s officially time to start thinking about Week 1, the Dallas Cowboys and the rest of the 2026 campaign.
Of course, new coach John Harbaugh has been thinking about those things since he arrived in New York. While it remains to be seen what kind of team the Giants
full_text:
New York Giants coach John Harbaugh isn't afraid to call out his players in the media if they've made an avoidable mistake. Rich Storry / Imagn Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The preseason is over for the New York Giants, which means it’s officially time to start thinking about Week 1, the Dallas Cowboys and the rest of the 2026 campaign.
Of course, new coach John Harbaugh has been thinking about those things since he arrived in New York. While it remains to be seen what kind of team the Giants will ultimately become under Harbaugh, there’s one thing he’s made clear throughout the preseason: If the Giants are going to lose, it will not be because they’ve beaten themselves with silly mistakes.
He will not tolerate that.
“A lot of times, if somebody does make a mistake,” linebacker Micah McFadden said after Friday’s preseason finale, “they’ll get pulled from that play … like, ‘Hey, you got to lock in.'”
Harbaugh’s intolerance for avoidable mistakes goes beyond just yanking players off the field. He’s willing to vent his frustrations publicly, too. Consider the way he’s handled the few dustups during camp; consider the way he chose to talk about running back Cam Skattebo this past week.
Everyone knows Skattebo brings his big personality to the field every day, and typically, that audacious personality is welcomed by his teammates and coaches, including Harbaugh. As the second-year running back has worked his way back from the gruesome ankle injury he suffered last season, his ceaseless energy has been on full display all spring and summer. Skattebo could often be heard across the field during camp as he hyped up teammates and talked trash with the Giants defense.
But in the final open practice of Giants training camp, Skattebo let his passion get the better of him — at least according to Harbaugh. After catching a pass and sliding to the ground late in the practice, Skattebo ended up in a skirmish with Giants defensive backs Jevon Holland and Greg Newsome II.
It resulted in a flag for the Giants offense.
After practice, Harbaugh was asked about the energy Skattebo brings to the team and whether it’s “infectious.”
“Skatt’s great,” Harbaugh said. “He does bring a lot of energy. But he did get a 15-yard penalty at the end of practice. Did you notice that? That’s not infectious. Well, it is infectious, actually. Infectious in a bad way, right? Like an infectious disease type of thing. We don’t want that. We want it to be directed in a positive way.”
Despite Skattebo’s admitted tendency to, as he said while referring to his ill-fated backflip at Fanatics Fest, “do some dumb things,” he hasn’t been the only subject of Harbaugh’s ire.
Let’s rewind a little further back, to early August when starting quarterback Jaxson Dart flipped a ball at cornerback Newsome after throwing a touchdown pass. When asked about that incident after practice, Harbaugh didn’t talk about Dart’s competitive edge and swagger. He talked about sending a message.
“I think it’s a 15-yard penalty for taunting, so we backed up the extra point and had to do it again,” a clearly irritated Harbaugh said. “Did you see that? That’s how we handled it.”
Even without saying anything, the coach has been clear about the lines he’s drawing, with penalties being enforced even in practice.
“I think he understands that for the game-winning extra point, we don’t want it to be a 50-yard extra point,” Harbaugh said of the Dart incident. “Do you think I need to say anything (to him) in that case? Pretty clear-cut, right?”
Ahead of joint practices in Miami with the Dolphins, Harbaugh enforced game day rules regarding fights. And, of course, with high temperatures and humidity, tempers boiled over a few times. Following his involvement in a fight, right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor ended up watching the final drive of the practice from the sidelines.
“Anybody that threw a punch in the scrimmages would be treated like a game,” Harbaugh said.
While Eluemunor’s punch wasn’t hard, it was to the face, and as Harbaugh said, “That’ll get you in the game.”
Of course, there’s no guarantee Harbaugh’s no-nonsense approach will translate seamlessly to the regular season. But it’s worth pointing out that despite the few examples we’ve highlighted, Harbaugh’s message about the Giants not beating themselves seems to have largely taken hold. After 21 grueling practices , it says something that the only intrasquad “fight” we’ve seen came on the last day (the Skattebo incident).
“Penalties are like the first thing we watch together … in a team meeting after the next day of practice,” Giants guard Jon Runyan said after Friday’s preseason finale. “I mean, they’re sticklers for it.”
The Giants could use a little more discipline than they’ve shown in the past. Last year, the Giants committed the third-most accepted penalties in the NFL (128), costing themselves 1,075 yards — the league average was 108 accepted penalties and 870 yards.
Harbaugh’s Ravens, meanwhile, were far better than average in that department. They only committed 99 accepted penalties, costing them 746 yards.
“Obviously, no coach likes penalties,” Giants guard Jon Runyan said Friday. “But this has been the biggest emphasis on no penalties I’ve ever been around.”
Since arriving in New York, Harbaugh has often been described as a floor-raising head coach. While that can sometimes be a nebulous term, his fixation on cutting out mistakes — and the harmful penalties that come with them — is tangible evidence of exactly how Harbaugh is trying to raise the floor in New York.

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — At the beginning of training camp, Aaron Glenn said he “liked” where the Jets were — but he wanted to love where they’re at.

full_text:
Jason Sanders outlasted Cade York, but his recent struggles could have the Jets looking elsewhere for a kicker. Adam Hunger / AP
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — At the beginning of training camp, Aaron Glenn said he “liked” where the Jets were — but he wanted to love where they’re at.
Training camp and the preseason are over, and it does feel like the Jets have made some strides across the board. Geno Smith is a clear upgrade at quarterback. The offense has some weapons. The defense added veteran stability in free agency and talent in the NFL Draft — it showed during practices, joint practices and in game situations.
Now that camp is over, how does Glenn feel?
“Still in that process right now,” Glenn said. “But I do like where we’re at now.”
The next step in the process will be Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey trimming the roster down from 90 players to 53 ahead of Sunday’s deadline.
Here’s our final projection at what that might look like when the initial cuts come through:
In: Geno Smith, Cade Klubnik Out: Brady Cook, Bailey Zappe
Not much new here. Smith is and will remain the Jets’ starter. The hope is that Klubnik doesn’t have to play, but for now, he is the no-doubt No. 2. Zappe and Cook didn’t push Klubnik for the job, so now we wait to see if Mougey wants to scoop up a quarterback from another roster, via trade or the waiver wire.
Klubnik is a rookie with some moxie. He should be capable of managing the offense, though it would be better if he didn’t have to anytime soon. He struggled a bit in the preseason finale — especially on an interception he threw in the second quarter on a pass intended for Jelani Woods. He finished 6 of 13 for 59 yards and no touchdowns, and 21 of 34 for 197 yards and zero touchdowns in three preseason games.
When Glenn was asked if Klubnik won the No. 2 job, he said: “We’re going to sit back and evaluate that … we’ll take a look at that and make the right decision.”
In: Breece Hall, Braelon Allen, Isaiah Davis, Kene Nwangwu Out: Andrew Beck, Chip Trayanum, Dominic Richardson
I’ve had the hardest time figuring out if Beck sticks around. Ultimately, here’s where I landed: He will likely receive safe passage to the practice squad, and the Jets can use an elevation on him for a couple of weeks if they view him as a necessity for special teams or as a blocking specialist on offense. I would be less likely that someone like tight end Jelani Woods could make it through waivers after the way he’s played this summer.
Hall is injured but should be fine for Week 1. I’m less confident in Davis, and Nwangwu doesn’t bring much to the table at running back — I do wonder if the Jets bring in someone off the waiver wire, or add someone mildly notable to the practice squad in case Davis isn’t ready after missing most of training camp with a knee injury.
In: Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper, Isaiah Williams, Tim Patrick, Arian Smith Out: Malik McClain, Jamaal Pritchett, Cam Camper, Quincy Skinner, Junior Bergen
I put Patrick in the Beck bucket. The Jets can probably safely pass him through to the practice squad if they want. Patrick has gotten minimal snaps with the first-team offense and didn’t exactly make a significant impact in his snaps with Klubnik either. A sign that he’s safe, though: He sat out Friday night’s game while Smith played.
As for Smith: If there was anyone on the roster seriously pushing for his spot, he would be cut, but he does have a role on special teams, so this isn’t a Malachi Corley situation (and the Jets did just draft Smith in the fourth round a year ago). If anyone in the “out” group was going to have a shot to stick around, I’d say it’s McClain, who has had some moments and made some plays on special teams, or Pritchett if the Jets decided they’d rather he return kicks than Nwangwu.
Of this group, I’d at least expect McClain and Pritchett to land on the practice squad.
In: Mason Taylor, Kenyon Sadiq, Jeremy Ruckert, Jelani Woods Out: Chase Curtis, Connor Hulstein
This looks like the best and deepest tight end room the Jets have had in a long time, maybe since the Dustin Keller era. Taylor came on strong at the end of camp and looks like a legitimate TE1, Ruckert had his best summer as a pro catching the ball and Woods played his way onto the roster (he’s also a favorite of offensive coordinator Frank Reich).
As for Sadiq: The Jets will have to throttle back their plans for him to start the season after he missed most of the summer due to aggravating a hernia injury. He could be ready for Week 1 but probably not in a significant role. Still, don’t sleep on him making an impact later in the year.
“There’s no doubt we’ll have to scale it back,” Reich said. “You just got to work him in slowly, can’t rush it as much as we would like to. The good thing is he’s very smart — and we’ve said it all before, and he’ll be as ready as you can go — but there’s nothing like practice. I know he’s stayed locked in, but we got to get back on the practice field and just slowly work him back into the mix.”
Curtis should stick on the practice squad.
In: Olu Fashanu, Armand Membou, Dylan Parham, Joe Tippmann, Josh Myers, Chukwuma Okorafor, Anez Cooper, Max Mitchell, Xavier Newman Out: Landon Young, Kohl Levao, Cortland Ford, Xavier Hill, Marquis Hayes, Liam Fornadel
Maybe the Jets feel comfortable with Newman as their backup center, but I think they’ll have some options on the waiver wire for depth at the pivot. Newman struggled snapping the ball all summer and the Jets would prefer not to move Tippmann back to center if Myers gets hurt. The rest of the group behind the starters feels relatively safe.
Cooper suffered a shoulder injury on Friday and was promptly declared out. If it’s a multiple-week injury, he’ll be an IR candidate since he’s not expected to have much of a role just yet. If that’s the case, Levao (who can play center) would be a candidate to stick around. As would Young (who has 56 games of experience, including 12 starts).
In: T’Vondre Sweat, David Onyemata, Harrison Phillips, Jowon Briggs, Darrell Jackson Out: Payton Page, Mazi Smith, Jack Heflin, Junior Tafuna
This group has been locked in all summer. Sweat finally returned and his impact on the running game is undeniable. Onyemata has not made plays at all this summer, but he’s beloved by the coaching staff. Jackson was one of the summer surprises and has played his way into a possible rotational role.
Page and Heflin have had their moments and should stick on the practice squad if they aren’t claimed on waivers.
In: David Bailey, Kingsley Enagbare, Joe Ossai, Will McDonald, Nate Lynn Out: Braiden McGregor, Paschal Ekeji, Anthony Dunn PUP: Tyler Baron
Enagbare was another pleasant surprise this summer and feels like the best bet to start opposite Bailey, though how the Jets deploy this group might depend on the situation. McDonald had a very quiet summer; he will get work on obvious passing downs. Enagbare thrives against the run, though he’s a better pass rusher than I expected. Ossai is unique in that he can also slide inside at linebacker if needed.
Lynn is a really fun story. He signed a little over a week ago, promptly got two sacks against the Steelers, another sack in practice a few days later and then another sack against the Giants in the preseason finale. Maybe he came on too late to stick around, but at this point I’m not positive he won’t get claimed on waivers if the Jets cut him. He’s played well enough over the last 10 days, and it can’t hurt that he was with Glenn in Detroit in 2024.
“He’s just taking advantage of his opportunity,” Glenn said. “That’s another tape we have to evaluate to see if he put himself in position. He’s done a hell of a job, I know that … that’s hard to ignore.”
In reality, McGregor is probably more likely to make it than Lynn, but I’m buying into Lynn’s momentum.
In: Demario Davis, Jamien Sherwood, Kiko Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball, Mykal Walker Out: Chase Wilson, Jaden Keller
Another obvious spot…

full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles QB Andy Dalton and RB Carson Steele are both fighting for roster spots ahead of Sunday's cutdown day. Isaiah Vazquez / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Training camp is over. The preseason film is filed. The Philadelphia Eagles now must choose their 53-man roster and 16-man practice squad by the NFL’s 6 p.m. ET Sunday deadline.
The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena make their final roster predictions.
Kubena (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton
This is as precarious as the quarterback depth has been in coach Nick Sirianni’s tenure. There was no clear winner in the backup battle between Tanner McKee and Andy Dalton. Both quarterbacks fared better against the opponent’s third-team defenses in the last two exhibitions. McKee had his chance to seize the QB2 spot by starting against the Cincinnati Bengals on Friday night, and he went 12 of 22 passing for 55 yards and an interception. Unless GM Howie Roseman makes a trade here, it behooves the Eagles to keep Dalton around on the practice squad. McKee, a 2023 sixth-round pick, would be subject to waivers if cut.
Worth noting: Cole Payton was in the backfield with the punt coverage team. It appears the Eagles, who liked Payton’s athleticism coming out of North Dakota State, are finding additional value in the fifth-round rookie if they keep him on the 53-man roster.
Berman (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton
This could go in any direction. Neither McKee nor Dalton did enough to win the No. 2 job. Does McKee keep it based on what he’s demonstrated in Philadelphia in the past? Does Dalton stay because of experience — or does that enhance his trade value to a backup-needy team? Then again, the Eagles might be a backup-needy team. Would Roseman seek a trade of his own — Anthony Richardson or J.J. McCarthy are former first-rounders who could benefit from a change of scenery. Roseman could also keep all four quarterbacks to maintain his bluff. That covers all the possibilities, which suggests a lack of clarity after five weeks of training camp.  Payton has more versatility than a typical depth quarterback, which could make him an intriguing option to develop a Taysom Hill-like role.
Kubena (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley
This trio was never truly challenged in training camp. Carson Steele had an impressive game against the Patriots and recorded another touchdown catch against the Bengals. Dameon Pierce, debuting after missing time with a hamstring injury, showcased his power running style by gaining 44 yards on four carries. There doesn’t seem to be room for either player on this initial roster. But they could make for interesting additions to the practice squad — and useful foils for the defense as members of the scout team unit.
Berman (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley
These three are all locks, as evidenced by Nick Sirianni keeping the trio sidelined for the final game. Both Carson Steele and Dameon Pierce showed ability during the preseason, but I don’t see the Eagles keeping more than three.
Kubena (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper
Darius Cooper did not suit up Friday night — an indication that he has all but sealed a spot on the 53-man roster for a second straight year. Cooper has graduated from the feel-good training camp story. It will be interesting to see how much he progresses as a pass-catcher in Year 2. Elijah Moore did suit up Friday and is a sensible practice-squad option because none of his $1.3 million contract is guaranteed. The Eagles can pick up a roster spot if they keep Moore in town.
Berman (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown
These five should all be on the team, with Brown’s $5 million guaranteed contract and his quality experience helping his case. Cooper has been a training camp standout who went from the roster bubble to sitting in the final preseason game. The question is whether they keep another receiver such as Moore. I think he’s more likely as a practice squad elevation.
Kubena (3): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers
There is little question about the efficacy of Goedert and Mundt when they are both on the field. But it does not yet look like the Eagles can rely on Stowers to provide them with the depth they need at this position. The second-round rookie still needs to progress as a blocker. It also does not help that he missed the last three training camp practices, plus Friday night’s preseason finale, with a hamstring injury. Is the best backup on the roster? Practice squad mainstays Cam Latu and E.J. Jenkins both have dropped passes in training camp. Stone Smartt totaled seven catches for 47 yards in the final two exhibitions.
Berman (4): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers, Cameron Latu
Stowers has had a quiet camp, and an injury last week kept him out of the preseason finale. Depending on the severity of Stowers’ injury, pay attention to his roster status to begin the season. Latu has not necessarily excelled this summer and is the last player on this 53-man roster, but his special teams value and versatility as a fullback put him on the list. It wouldn’t surprise me if Roseman seeks an upgrade for the tight end depth chart — especially with the Eagles expected to play heavy packages. Do the Eagles call Zach Ertz and allow him to finish his career in Philadelphia?
Kubena (10): Lane Johnson, Jordan Mailata, Markel Bell, Fred Johnson, Cam Jurgens, Landon Dickerson, Tyler Steen, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris
The rookie Bell missed the final three training camp practices and the preseason finale with a thumb/leg injury. This underscores why it makes sense for the Eagles to keep Fred Johnson on the roster as another capable option. Lampkin and Kendall’s strong showing in training camp showed the Eagles can feel confident in their interior backup options. Neither player suited up Friday, which should be taken as a vote of confidence. Will the Eagles need to call upon them this year?
Berman (10): Jordan Mailata, Landon Dickerson, Cam Jurgens, Tyler Steen, Lane Johnson, Fred Johnson, Markel Bell, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris
Fred Johnson is a tough one to figure in this group — especially if Bell is the Eagles’ swing tackle. Fred Johnson could be a trade candidate or even a practice squad player considering he’s a vested veteran. Still, I have him on this 53-man roster to give the Eagles an experienced offensive tackle. Otherwise, the reserves are inexperienced. The Eagles’ interior offensive linemen have demonstrated impressive development this summer; Kendall, Lampkin, and Morris all made strides. I’m watching to see if the Eagles keep Cameron Williams and Myles Hinton for developmental purposes, although neither has shown enough.
Kubena (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Zion Wilson
I am adding Wilson for the first time. The undrafted rookie from East Carolina finished training camp with a series of impressive practices and recorded a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit in the preseason finale. I think he offers the Eagles more immediate value than Uar Bernard, who defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has said is “light years away” from contributing. Yes, it would be a risk to subject Bernard to the waiver wire. But acquiring him would be a considerable investment for any team. The Eagles could then keep him on their practice squad without counting him against the numbers as a member of the International Pathway Program.
Berman (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Uar Bernard
Carter, Davis and Ojomo form a trio of DTs at or near the top of the league, while Young is a quality reserve. Bernard was drafted as a long-term project, and I don’t expect the Eagles to expose him to waivers and risk another team absorbing the project. full_text:
Trevon Diggs was all smiles after intercepting a pass in his first game as a Seahawk on Friday in Kansas City. Reed Hoffmann / Associated Press
The Athletic has live coverage of Saturday’s NFL preseason action.
The Seattle Seahawks wrapped up their preseason with a 9-9 tie with the Kansas City Chiefs on Friday night at Arrowhead Stadium, as kicker Jason Myers’ 52-yard field goal attempt on the final play sailed wide.
Second-year quarterback Jalen Milroe started and played the entire game as Seattle rested its starters on both sides of the ball. Milroe turned in what was perhaps his most impressive performance since the Seahawks selected him in the third round in 2025, completing 16 of 26 passes for 223 yards and a touchdown pass to tight end Nick Vannett.
“I thought Jalen Milroe played a really good game,” coach Mike Macdonald told reporters. “Took care of the football, was decisive. Made some really strong throws down the field. Put us in a really strong position to win there at the end.”
Wide receiver Cody White stood out with a team-high three catches for 69 yards, including a 40-yard bomb from Milroe hauled in between two defenders. Veteran cornerback Trevon Diggs bolstered his argument to be Seattle’s third cornerback with a strong debut, highlighted by an interception of Chiefs quarterback Garrett Nussmeier.
“Did some great things today,” Macdonald said of Diggs, who signed with Seattle just over a week earlier . “Obviously, having the interception was pretty awesome. But I’ve been really impressed since he got here.”
Aside from a few key battles, most of Seattle’s 53-man roster, which must be finalized by 3 p.m. PT Sunday, appears set. This is my projection of how it will look on Sunday.
Notes: The projection includes several players who could go to injured reserve with a designation to return. Only two players can be given that designation before the cutdown deadline, which could mean additional transactions Monday. Rookies in italics.
Seattle will run it back not only with the same trio of quarterbacks, but with them in the same order on the depth chart as 2025.
Darnold will be under center again when the regular season gets underway, and Lock earned the right to retain his role as the No. 2 quarterback. In two preseason games, he completed 21 of 27 passes for 143 yards and two touchdowns.
Meanwhile, Milroe remains a green player with plenty of room to grow. He flashed his athleticism several times, like when rushing for 36 yards on five carries against the Dallas Cowboys in the preseason opener, but he still needs some polish as a passer. He tossed two interceptions against the Tennessee Titans before bouncing back Friday.
Barring injuries, Seattle has depth at quarterback, so it’s not much of an issue that Milroe still needs more seasoning. Friday’s performance was particularly noteworthy for Milroe, who had shown little evidence he could be trusted in a regular-season game.
“Definitely felt like he took a step in his game,” Macdonald said. “He should be excited about his growth.”
Cut: Velus Jones Jr., Justin Jones, Brock Lampe
Price did not appear in the preseason after missing time in training camp with what Macdonald described as “upper-leg soreness,” though he returned to practice in recent weeks. That shouldn’t stop Seattle’s first-round rookie from making an immediate impact once the regular season gets underway, or at the very least from splitting time with Holani.
Holani could be Seattle’s No. 1 running back for the season opener. The third-year pro is revered for his pass blocking and has the frame (5-foot-10, 208 pounds) for short-yardage situations.
Wright, who had a 69-yard touchdown run against the Titans, should make the roster. However, that’s assuming Wilson remains sidelined with a hamstring injury. Wilson is a candidate for injured reserve, which would keep him out for at least four weeks and save Seattle a roster spot in the meantime.
On Friday, Macdonald said Wilson will be back at some point this season.
Charbonnet, who tore his ACL during the playoffs, will likely remain on the physically unable to perform list and miss at least four regular-season games. He would be eligible to practice after Week 2.
Russell will be Seattle’s fullback with Robbie Ouzts out for the entire season because of a neck injury.
IR : Tory Horton, Irv Charles
Cut: Ricky White III, Rashad Rochelle , Julian Hicks
Smith-Njigba, Kupp and Shaheed are locks. After them, several combinations would make sense for Seattle’s depth wideouts.
Foster, in his second season from Michigan State, makes this cut following the loss of Jake Bobo, who will miss the season with a torn ACL. Horton is a candidate to start the season on injured reserve, considering he has not practiced recently due to an undisclosed injury.
Horton’s and Bobo’s absences could also clear a path for Henderson and Cody White. Henderson, a sixth-round rookie, might have the chance to contribute on special teams, which is perhaps what he does best, having returned kicks at Kansas. He also had three catches for 58 yards on Friday.
White, Seattle’s biggest receiver at 6-3, 227 pounds, has a spot on the roster because he offers a very different skill set from the rest of the wideouts. A strong preseason finale hardly hurt his cause.
After a breakout second season in the pros, Barner has separated himself as Seattle’s No. 1 tight end.
Arroyo was slowed by injuries at times in his rookie season but should take on a more prominent role in first-year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury’s offense. Fleury likes to use multiple tight ends, which could mean plenty of playing time for Saubert, who played for Fleury in San Francisco.
Kallerup’s youth makes him a more logical candidate over Vannett, who is entering his 11th NFL season.
Cut: G Christian Haynes, OT Amari Kight, OT Bobby Hart, OT Derrick Graham , OT Logan Brown, C Federico Maranges
Much has changed since Seattle’s offensive line was viewed as one of the weakest in the NFL as recently as 2024, when they allowed 54 sacks, tied for third most in the league. The Seahawks return all five starters from last year’s unit, which kept Darnold upright all season, along with key reserves like Jones, Oluwatimi, and youngsters Stephens and Cabeldue, each a recent draft pick. Hart, who has started 75 NFL games, comes up short of making the roster.
Cut: Deven Eastern, J.R. Singleton, Bubba Thomas, Uso Seumalo
Aside from Mills making the opening-night roster, Seattle will roll out essentially the same interior defensive line as in 2025.
Mills, who missed nearly all of the 2025 season recovering from an ACL injury suffered in college, has moved around well in training camp and is poised for a more prominent role in 2026.
Otherwise, it’s the status quo for a unit that is too deep to bring longer-term projects like Seumalo aboard.
Cut: Jared Ivey, Connor O’Toole, Jamie Sheriff, Jalan Gaines, Marvin Jones Jr., Aidan Hubbard
Few position groups for the Seahawks are as talented as outside linebacker, where the four projected to make the roster have combined for a whopping 170 1/2 career sacks.
Seattle should manage without Boye Mafe, who signed with the Cincinnati Bengals in free agency.
O’Toole and Ivey both made the team last year, though, so it’s not inconceivable that Seattle elects to keep one or both of the second-year pros instead of an extra safety or cornerback.
Cut: Patrick O’Connell, Aaron Smith, Power Echols
Surratt and O’Connell received plenty of playing time last season, logging nine and 11 games, respectively. However, the emergence of Thomas, who was the Seahawks’ second-leading tackler last season, and the continued development of Knight, who had 10 tackles in Seattle’s preseason loss to Dallas, create a roster crunch at this position.
Surratt and O’Connell each profile as special teamers first, so keeping only one makes sense. O’Connell might have improved his odds of sticking around by tying for the team lead with eight tackles Friday.

title: Final Commanders roster projection: Tough choice at WR, help needed on O-line Injuries have altered the calculus for Washington's initial 53-man roster, which is likely to change before the Sept. 13 season opener. Nicki Jhabvala 22
summary:
Washington coach Dan Quinn's initial 53-man roster is likely to change before the season opener. Tommy Gilligan / Imagn Images
In the 237 days since last season ended, the Commanders have overhauled their systems, replaced their play callers, and changed some of their coaching staff and much of their roster in hopes of rediscovering a winning formula.
The team that made it to the NFC Championship Game two years ago is once again in rebuild mode — but with higher stakes. Coach Dan Quinn’s future
full_text:
Washington coach Dan Quinn's initial 53-man roster is likely to change before the season opener. Tommy Gilligan / Imagn Images
In the 237 days since last season ended, the Commanders have overhauled their systems, replaced their play callers, and changed some of their coaching staff and much of their roster in hopes of rediscovering a winning formula.
The team that made it to the NFC Championship Game two years ago is once again in rebuild mode — but with higher stakes. Coach Dan Quinn’s future in Washington may depend on a winning season, and the window to build around quarterback Jayden Daniels while he’s on his rookie contract will soon close.
The Commanders’ revamped roster showed promise early in training camp, especially on defense, where the team made its biggest offseason investments. But a slew of injuries to starters and some key reserves limited their on-field work together and created uncertainty about who will be available when the season opens Sept. 13 in Philadelphia.
That also made the team’s initial 53-man roster, due by 6 p.m. Sunday, vulnerable to significant change before that first game. Washington is seventh in the NFL’s waiver list priority order, which means it’ll have a fairly early crack at claiming, say, an interior offensive lineman (or two) or landing other quality players waived by other teams.
My initial roster projection for Washington is just that — an early iteration but not the final roster for Week 1.
(Note: NFL teams can designate for return up to two players who are placed on injured reserve on roster cutdown day. Those count toward teams’ maximum of eight IR players designated for return, but do not count against the team’s roster cap. They are eligible to return after four games. Anyone else placed on injured reserve before the 6 p.m. deadline on Sunday is done for the season.)
Hey, shocker, Daniels is still the starter! In all seriousness, Daniels had an exceptional camp. He’s shown more and more every offseason, but this one was especially notable because of the new scheme and all that he was asked to change or do more of in offensive coordinator David Blough’s system. His transition to playing more under center appeared seamless, and his command of the offense was what you’d expect from a veteran with multiple years in a scheme.
Mariota returned on a one-year deal, ensuring continuity in the quarterback room amid all the other offensive changes.
The notable name here, though, is Kaliakmanis, a seventh-round rookie from Rutgers whose play in the first two preseason games earned him a spot here. Washington kept three quarterbacks on its initial roster the last two seasons, and with Mariota recovering from an MCL sprain, doing so again may be wise. Quinn has said he’s optimistic the veteran will be available for Week 1, but it’s not yet a certainty.
Whether Kaliakmanis sticks at the No. 3 for the season may depend on who comes available after roster cuts.
Washington released veteran Jerome Ford with an injury settlement and Jeremy McNichols suffered a “pretty good quad injury” in camp, according to Quinn. I didn’t include him on the belief he would clear waivers and be available to re-sign to the practice squad.
Allen had an up-and-down preseason — he had 85 rushing yards and a touchdown against Miami but fumbled on Washington’s opening snap in Baltimore — but his potential and draft status (sixth-round pick) ensure he stays. Undrafted rookie Robert Henry impressed in the opener against Miami, but he may not have shown enough to put Washington at risk of losing him on waivers.
Receiver was one of Washington’s most questionable positions before training camp, but the arrival of Diggs turned it into one of the most competitive.
McLaurin, Diggs and third-round rookie Williams were locks for the roster, leaving eight wideouts vying for three or four spots. Brown got the nod because of his speed and rapport with Daniels. Burks’ big-play ability won him a spot, and Lane made it because of his punt returns. I admittedly waffled about keeping McCaffrey. He had a very good camp and doubles as the team’s leading kick returner, but I wondered if he showed enough to hold his spot. I kept him because of his draft status (third round in 2024), his consistency compared to others and the value he provides over, say, a fifth linebacker or 10th offensive lineman.
It was always going to be these four. Yankoff had a good camp, showing his pass-catching ability on offense while remaining a special teams staple, and the others were locks before camp opened.
* Laremy Tunsil placed on injured reserve with a designation to return
This is the group that figures to change before the opener. It needs to change. Washington cut center Tyler Biadasz in February and didn’t sign another veteran in the offseason, essentially leaving the job to Allegretti, a versatile vet who has played primarily guard. But a calf injury sidelined Allegretti for almost all of camp and his status for the opener is still not clear. Also unclear: His ability as a full-time starter at center.
Julian Good-Jones and Gulbin, a sixth-round rookie, struggled mightily in place of Allegretti, hindering the run game and leaving Daniels exposed for much of the Commanders’ joint practice with the Ravens.
Gulbin stays on the roster largely because the team invested a draft pick in him, but it wasn’t a high enough one to keep him here long-term. Washington should add another center and more help at guard since Coleman shifted back outside to left tackle after Tunsil’s injury.
Tunsil is an obvious candidate for IR with a designation for return on cutdown day. He underwent surgery to repair a torn triceps on Aug. 8, but the team left open the possibility of him returning this season . That injury typically has a 3 to 4-month recovery, depending on the severity and type of repair.
*Johnny Newton is placed on IR with a designation to return.
Newton’s pectoral muscle injury will land him on IR, but, like Tunsil, there’s still a chance he could be available later this season, so designating him for return on cutdown day keeps the door open for Washington.
The Commanders brought back Settle and signed Omenihu to add needed depth at the position. Newton’s injury pushes Tuttle up as the top reserve.
Cowart gets the last spot because of his experience, but like others near the bottom of the depth chart, his spot could change depending on roster needs and who becomes available.
There are no real surprises here. Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho were possibilities for a fifth linebacker spot, but both seem likely to clear waivers, meaning Washington could sign them back to the practice squad and continue to develop them and have them ready for a few game-day call-ups.
*Dorance Armstrong is placed on the reserve/suspended list
The NFL suspended Armstrong for the season opener for violating the personal conduct policy, which temporarily clears a roster spot. Jean-Baptiste missed much of last season due to a pectoral injury and didn’t show much in the early going of camp. If Washington’s outside linebackers finished camp healthy and available, Jean-Baptiste may have been hard-pressed to get a spot, but Armstrong’s suspension and injuries to Oweh (calf) and Chaisson (knee) — Quinn has not provided a timetable for their return — make it worth keeping him.
There are a number of outstanding questions about this group, none bigger than the availability of Amos. The 2025 second-round pick was Washington’s most consistent corner last year, but a fractured fibula cut his season short and cost him the entire offseason. He returned two weeks into camp but suffered an ankle sprain in his second practice. It’s unclear if he will be available for Week 1.
Washington added Douglas and Moreau to give the team more veteran experience and depth, and both proved their worth.
Whenever Amos returns, it’ll be interesting to see whether Robertson or Sainristil shifts inside to the slot.
Washington’s most notable roster…

title: Ranking the Good, Bad and Ugly From Cardinals’ Loss to Packers
full_text:
It was a thrilling battle that went down to the final seconds.
The Arizona Cardinals leave Green Bay with a 42-38 loss after the Packers took the lead with just 20 seconds remaining, ensuring Matt LaFleur got the best of his younger brother Mike in the process.
Starters didn't play — but we've still got plenty to analyze from tonight.
Rating the good, bad and ugly from tonight's battle at Lambeau:
There's no other way to say it: The Cardinals' offense looks massively improved over its prior iterations.
LaFleur's worked wonders with this unit, and it's clear the offense is operating at a high level regardless of who is under center in Arizona. The Cardinals had 323 yards of offense in the first half alone before finishing with 492 net yards.
There's a reason the Cardinals have hit the over on their projected point totals in every preseason matchup. Rushing lanes are being paved while quarterbacks, 1-4 on the depth chart, have made plays. Such was the case in Green Bay tonight with Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis running the show.
Especially against a Packers defense coached by former head coach Jonathan Gannon, Cardinals fans should feel great about how the offense looks after tonight.
Imagine how much better things will be when all of the starters are finally in the saddle.
For as good as the offense was, it felt like Minshew and Slovis were consistently under pressure throughout the night.
Yes, backups were playing. It won't be a direct reflection of how the regular season will look, and Arizona did lose their top backup in Chase Bisontis while fellow interior offensive lineman Jon Gaines didn't suit up, either.
It was mostly Slovis who was on the receiving end of Green Bay's pressure. Whether it be the three sacks, ten quarterback hits or numerous tipped passes, Arizona failed to truly protect him through large stints of the night — even with an incredible rushing attack.
Not ideal, regardless of who's playing. The Packers getting home and forcing turnovers on mostly four-man fronts is quite sobering.
The Cardinals allowed what might have been one of the easiest punt returns in recent NFL memory back for a touchdown when Will Sheppard housed it 81 yards for the score.
ALL. THE. WAY. 81-YD PUNT RETURN FOR WILL SHEPPARD! 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/OIrsyTFZL0
Players slipped, were out of position and took bad angles to practically form teach tape on what not to do on punt coverage. Sheppard, despite initially blowing past three Cardinals defenders, wasn't touched nor was he close to having a finger on him during the return.
Special teams doesn't matter... until it does. Until something like this happens during a game, shifting momentum to the other side while allowing points in the process.
You'd be hard-pressed to find worse coverage than that play from the Cardinals, and new special teams coordinator Michael Ghobrial will be sure to let the players know in the film room tomorrow.

title: Cardinals WR, Fighting For Roster Spot, Ruled Out With Injury vs Packers
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals have ruled out wide receiver Ihmir Smith-Marsette for the remainder of action against the Green Bay Packers, according to AZCardinals.com's Darren Urban.
Smith-Marsette suffered an ankle injury in the third quarter of play and hobbled to the sideline before being ruled out. He caught two passes for 41 yards and manned return duties for the Cardinals tonight.
Names such as Simi Fehoko and Jalen Brooks — both of whom Smith-Marsette is competing with for a roster spot — are likely to see more time for the rest of action. The Cardinals have until Sunday at 3:00 PM AZ time to trim their roster down to 53.
Whether Smith-Marsette cracks that list remains to be determined. He was an early training camp breakout candidate, though Brooks' stellar play during preseason games saw Smith-Marsette take a slight step back.
He did not crack our final 53-man roster projection this week and was a dud for the first half of Cardinals vs Packers action.
Smith-Marsette is Arizona's second return man behind receiver Devin Duvernay, who did not dress tonight alongside 40 other Cardinals. Smith-Marsette' participation against the Packers clearly signals he's on the roster bubble.
There's going to be some extremely tough decisions made by the Cardinals within the next two days, Smith-Marsette being near the forefront of said conversations. Veteran wideout Kendrick Bourne says it's been the room's goal this camp.
"The greatest thing we've all been saying: we're making it hard on the coaches. That's all we can do. We don't want to have a group that's tearing each other down. I want to build people up. We want to build each other up to make plays, and I think that's what's been happening," Bourne said.
"You see it, it's a lot of encouragement going on. So when the ball's in the air, everybody's rooting for you. You can feel when you're being rooted for, and when you're being doubted. It's a different feel when the ball's in the air, and I think that's what we've been building as a group. Everybody's confident that they will make the play. That we're rooting for each other. I think that's important.
"So we got a strong room, man. We tell each other every day, like we're making it hard on them. It's going to be hard decisions, and that's just the nature of the game. But that's how we play the game is to make it as hard on cut day as possible for the coaches."
We'll see if Smith-Marsette's injury plays a factor into any decisions by Arizona. If he doesn't make the roster, he will be subject to waivers, where any of the other 31 teams can claim him. If he goes unclaimed, the Cardinals can bring him back to their practice squad.

title: Studs, Duds for Cardinals During First Half at Packers
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers put together an entertaining half of football at Lambeau Field on Friday with the Packers leading 24-20.
Studs and duds from the first two quarters:
Minshew looked really impressive to finish his preseason, going 7-for-9 for 126 yards and one touchdown in two drives before being pulled for Kedon Slovis. Minshew was able to spread the ball around to a handful of receivers and even made some checks to successful run plays at the line of scrimmage.
Smith-Marsette is battling for a roster spot, though his fumbled punt to start his time in Green Bay didn't quite help those chances. The ball rolled out of bounds, though this isn't the first time he's put the ball on the ground in preseason play. He also failed to keep his feet in-bounds for what would have been a toe-tap catch.
Brooks continues to produce at high levels, as he shined in the first half to the tune of four receptions for 57 yards. Whether it be Minshew, Carson Beck or Kedon Slovis, Brooks continually has gotten open and will force the Cardinals into an incredibly tough decision this weekend.
Pryor, while the Cardinals were driving, had a Packers defender blow past him for an easy sack on Minshew, which forced Arizona into a 3rd-and-20 that ultimately saw the team kick a field goal instead of scoring a potential touchdown. He then allowed a Packers defensive lineman to get a free rush on Slovis, which led to an interception.
Pryor's already fighting for a roster spot, and the pressure/sack doesn't exactly help.
Leota scored a half-sack alongside BJ Ojulari in the second quarter, but has been far more impactful than the guy he's battling with in the outside linebackers room. Leota's logged three other pressures including a blown-up screen play and has looked strong thus far.
Fairweather was called for multiple penalties on Arizona's last drive of the second quarter, stalling the Cardinals' progress to try and get out of their own half of the field. Both were holding calls.

title: Why Carson Beck Isn't Playing in Cardinals vs Packers Game
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers are underway at Lambeau Field for some Friday night preseason action — and star rookie quarterback Carson Beck is sidelined as a non-participant.
The third-round pick, alongside starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett, isn't active for Arizona's finale due to a rib injury. Passers in Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis will push the Cardinals across the finish line tonight.
What's going on with Beck, and how serious is his injury?
Beck has only played in one preseason game for Arizona — which was the Pro Football Hall of Fame Game back in the first week of August.
He suffered the rib injury early in action against the Carolina Panthers but finished the game and practiced through the next week just fine before suddenly being ruled out of their next matchup (Week 1 vs Las Vegas) just hours before game time.
Head coach Mike LaFleur would go on to tell reporters soreness increased to uncomfortable levels with Beck. The Miami/Georgia product hasn't practiced since, missing preseason games against the Raiders and Dallas Cowboys, respectively.
Beck did have a throwing session after practice just a few days ago, which LaFleur described as "good" — though he wasn't on the field for the team's joint practice against Green Bay on Wednesday, which all but sealed his fate for tonight.
Beck impressed towards the end of training camp and against Carolina, so it was a bit of a disappointment to have one of their more exciting young players out due to injury.
With final roster cuts approaching on Sunday, some are curious to see if Arizona places Beck on injured reserve to begin the regular season. This would see Beck miss at least the first four games but would allow him ample time to heal with Brissett and Minshew ahead of him on the depth chart .
However, Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro dismissed those rumors, calling it "unlikely" that he lands on injured reserve. You can read more about that here .
The Cardinals aren't worried about Beck's development due to the injury:
"It's easy to magnify the quarterback position and the rookie and all that kind of stuff, but yeah, you get better at football by practicing and playing football. So when you're not out there, it's hard to get better, right?" LaFleur told reporters this week.
"So he's missed some days, but that's no different than the nose guard. That's no different than the receiver. That's no different than the left tackle, particularly for the younger guys. So it is what it is. Injuries are part of this thing, and he's a tough dude. Like I said, he battled through it for three or four practices before the discomfort became so real that it just wasn't worth it to [play] because it wasn't going to improve until we gave him a little bit of time."
After tonight, the Cardinals will have a week off before preparing for the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 1.

title: 10 Cardinals Facing Make-or-Break Moments in Preseason Finale
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals have one final preseason game for 2026, and though starters aren't expecting to play, there's still plenty on the line for several players across the roster.
Besides putting on good tape for potential teams once Sunday's flurry of roster moves happens, the Cardinals are still deciding on a few different key roster spots.
These ten Cardinals are in absolute make-or-break territory against the Green Bay Packers:
If the Cardinals do indeed keep a sixth receiver, this is a two-way battle that as of now tilts in Brooks' favor. Brooks has really come into his own across preseason play and has performed well against live competition.
That's not to say Smith-Marsette hasn't, though he was an early roster surprise during the initial stages of training camp before Brooks stole momentum. What do the Cardinals value more: offensive production or special teams value?
The Cardinals have their starting line set with a handful of pretty good bets to make the roster underneath as backups on the depth chart for both tackle and guard spots. Udoh has started at multiple OL spots during his career before signing with Arizona this offseason, but likely finds himself on the outside looking in.
Yet after Chase Bisontis went down with his likely season-ending injury, a spot has opened in the Cardinals' OL room. A strong outing from Udoh just might sway Arizona to add an extra body to the room.
This is a similar story to Udoh, but just on the other side of the trenches. Williams had been a spot starter early in his career before molding into a depth guy across NFL defensive line rooms. Arizona's six DL up front feels fairly concrete, especially with rookie Kaleb Proctor out for the season.
However, the door for Williams just might be open thanks to defensive coordinator Nick Rallis and his insistence on using a platoon of bodies along the defensive line. If Williams can make plays, perhaps that changes some conversations.
Ojulari's the biggest name on this list, and it's a shame considering how well he played during his rookie season prior to a severe knee injury. Arizona's former second-round pick has quietly faded into the depth of the Cardinals' OLB rotation, playing deep into all three preseason games.
Now, Ojulari very much finds himself on the ropes. He didn't make the team in our final roster projections with Eku Leota usurping him. Ojulari needs to put a cape on and rescue his roster spot.
The Cardinals are unlikely to keep five inside linebackers, placing the veteran Pappoe and rookie Sharar into a sort of battle not just for the ILB position, but a roster spot in general. Pappoe's speed and experience could give him the edge while Sharar's status as a fresh draft pick and untapped potential could see him land on the roster.
Much like other spots near the bottom of the 53, this will come down to special teams — which both are capable of contributing to.
The Cardinals' toughest decision just might come in the cornerback room, where Arizona has numerous capable bodies with little room to spare. There will, unfortunately, be some strong talent that slips through the cracks. As of now, Jones is likely the man to be cut with either of Clark or Thomas potentially joining, too.
Clark, Thomas and Jones all find themselves with a massive 60 minutes leading up to their time at Lambeau. A standout performance from any of the aforementioned corners can carry some heavy weight.

title: Three Bold Predictions for Cardinals vs Packers Preseason Finale
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers are hoping to put on a show to finish preseason festivities.
60 minutes of action at Lambeau Field is the only thing standing in the way of an important weekend for both teams, where the Cardinals and Packers will cut their rosters down to 53 ahead of the regular season.
Starters aren't expected to play tonight, opening the door for just about anything to happen with backups taking the field.
Three bold predictions for tonight:
The bottom of the Cardinals' WR room is in a tight race to compete for a potential WR6 spot in the desert with Jalen Brooks and Ihmir Smith-Marsette leading the way.
Brooks has recently gained momentum with strong outings in preseason games. Smith-Marsette had the early lead thanks to work with the Cardinals' starters on offense and special teams.
Both need to put a cherry on top of their work before roster cuts arrive Sunday, and that's not lost on either player. The good news? Arizona's offense has (mostly) been humming and players are capable of finding the end zone.
There's no Jacoby Brissett or Carson Beck tonight, paving the way for Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis to play snaps under center.
In fairness, all four quarterbacks have seen success running Mike LaFleur's offense. However, both Minshew and Slovis are prone to making mistakes — especially against an aggressive Jonathan Gannon-led defense (more on him in a minute).
Minshew's style of play is exactly that of a gun-slinger, a passer who isn't afraid to take chances. While that can lead to some exciting moments, that also places the ball in danger of heading the other way.
As for Slovis, he went just 2/7 passing against the Cowboys last weekend. He's staring down what is very likely his last bit of playing time for 2026, and he'll likely look to go down swinging before he's sent to waivers.
Who doesn't love a good revenge game?
Gannon was fired by the Cardinals this past offseason and now looks to rebound with the Super Bowl-ready Packers. There's a plethora of talent on both sides of the ball, including Micah Parsons returning at some point under Gannon.
Realistically, Gannon's not going to reveal exotic stuff tonight against his former team. It wouldn't be worth exposing film for the regular season.
Calling it bad blood between the two sides just might even be a stretch.
Still, Gannon likes to have a good time — and that just might include dialing up a bit more pressure than usual against a backup Cardinals OL that lost Chase Bisontis earlier in the preseason.

title: Cardinals vs. Packers: 2 Best Bets for Tonight's Preseason Finale
full_text:
It's nearly time for the Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers to square off at Lambeau Field for tonight's preseason finale for both sides.
With starters not expected to play , fans of Arizona and Green Bay are sure to see a handful of position battles finalize while players can make or break their chances of landing on the final roster.
Case in point, there's still plenty riding on tonight's game for both sides — and it should be plenty entertaining.
If you're looking for action tonight, here's two of the best bets we found on the internet:
Iain MacMillan, SI.com: "Instead of betting on a side in this game, I'm going to bet the OVER in the LaFleur Bowl. Both offenses have been strong so far in the postseason. The Cardinals have hung 30+ points in two of their three games, and the Packers are coming off a 33-point performance against the Broncos, who have one of the best defenses in the NFL.
"Quarterbacks for both teams have also been impressive thus far. Gardner Minshew has been great for the Cardinals, and Carson Beck is on track to get back on the field. The 2025 sixth-round pick Kyle McCord has also been good for the Packers. More often than not, good quarterback play is all a game needs to hit the OVER in a preseason affair.
"Let's sit back and root for points in this one."
Our take: We're not sure where MacMillan is getting his information, as Beck hasn't thrown a pass in practice in roughly two weeks and would be a massive surprise to play tonight. Though the Cardinals haven't officially ruled him out (since they're in Green Bay and not meeting with local reporters) the overwhelming expectation is Beck won't play.
Michael Crosson, Action Network: "In the chaotic preseason environment, public perception routinely overreacts to single-week scoring margins. By taking the moneyline on overlooked underdogs in tight-spread settings, bettors capitalize on market mispricings driven by public bias than actual on-field execution.
"... Our internal tracking shows early public action heavily skewed toward Green Bay, drawing 76% of bets and 93% of total money. In reality, the wrong team is likely favored here. Arizona possesses the superior backup quarterback tandem in Minshew and Slovis, an offense averaging over 240 passing yards per game through three preseason games, and the LaFleur brother who seems to have more personal incentive to compete.
"We'll fade the public overreaction and back the Cardinals on the moneyline."
Our take: Moneyline bets always feel like a toss-up in preseason, and with practically no starters playing in this game, it truly does feel like a coin-flip. What we can say about Arizona's offense is it hasn't mattered who operates it — it's looked fairly solid. With that said, Slovis didn't look exactly strong against the Dallas Cowboys last week.

title: How to Watch Cardinals' Preseason Finale vs. Packers (Start Time, Channel, Who to Monitor & More)
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' preseason is nearly over.
Just 60 minutes of football at Lambeau Field separates the Cardinals from the regular season. Neither Arizona or the Packers are expected to field their starters tonight, though with roster cut day approaching on Sunday, this might just be the Cardinals' most important battle of the preseason.
It's one more opportunity for head coach Mike LaFleur and his staff to evaluate the roster ahead of some tough decisions looming this weekend. This is also the final time LaFleur will be able to see his offense in live action before the wins and losses begin to count.
Here's everything you need to know ahead of Friday's Cardinals vs. Packers preseason finale, including how to watch and one important position to monitor.
One of the Cardinals' biggest debates is how many receivers the team will carry on their final 53-man roster. Big names such as Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne are obvious choices while new additions in Devin Duvernay and fifth-round pick Reggie Virgil feel safe, too.
If Arizona does keep a sixth wideout, Brooks and Smith-Marsette feel like the top two candidates competing for the job.
Smith-Marsette initially had the lead in this race after an impressive training camp, which featured some rotation with the first-team Cardinals offense on top of special teams duties. He's considered the secondary returner after Duvernay.
However, Brooks has built some serious momentum in recent weeks thanks to his performance in preseason games — making plays deep down the field and being a reliable target for multiple Cardinals quarterbacks between the white lines.
There's a possibility neither is chosen on Arizona's roster ( matching our 53-man roster prediction) , though that doesn't make tonight any less interesting: teams around the league will be watching film from the game, effectively making this a try-out ahead of a busy weekend across the NFL.

title: Latest Jeremiyah Love Update is What Cardinals Fans Want to Hear
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals lost star rookie running back Jeremiyah Love to a high ankle injury during preseason play — one that's not only kept him out for the remainder of exhibition action but possibly the team's regular season opener as well.
Love, who hasn't practiced since departing Las Vegas with his injury, is reportedly making good progress and is trending in the right direction to be available for Arizona's Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers.
"Jeremiyah Love trending in the right direction for week one needs to keep progressing though - still a ways to go but looking positive," Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro said of Love on a recent X post.
He also gave an update on Carson Beck — which you can read more about here .
Some Cardinals talk - Jeremiyah Love trending in the right direction for week one needs to keep progressing though - still a ways to go but looking positive. Carson Beck unlikely to start on IR - lost a chance at some valuable reps so that hurts we all were excited to see him…
Love tallied 14 total touches against the Raiders in what was likely his only glimpse of preseason action before LaFleur post-game described his ankle injury as something he likely could have returned with.
At the time, the Cardinals didn't seem worried about Love's injury. Love himself spoke with reporters in the locker room of Allegiant Stadium and seemed to be in good spirits.
Since the team returned from Vegas the injury seemingly regressed, and the Cardinals' running back room added another body to the sidelines with James Conner currently not playing/practicing and Trey Benson landing on injured reserve .
Love impressed in the short amount of time he played against the Raiders, stacking on top of an exciting training camp to generate legitimate buzz around the Valley.
He holds potential to be a game-changer for the Cardinals.
"He's doing well, progressing well, and kind of in the next phase of it," LaFleur said on Love earlier this week before confirming he wouldn't practice against the Packers.
Even as a rookie in a crowded backfield, Love figures to be a prominent part of Arizona's offense thanks to his ability to impact the rushing and receiving game at high levels.
“He really could come to our room if he ever wanted to,” Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. said of Love. “Seeing him on twitch routes killing backers is laughable sometimes.”
Between his injury and Week 1 in Los Angeles, Love will have had nearly a calander month to recover and prepare to play against the Chargers. It's likely even if Love is active, the Cardinals may ease his workload thanks to Tyler Allgeier's presence in the room.
